item.title: The security of US water systems is even leakier than we thought
item.description: American water systems are even less secure than we thought, according to a study of 236 technology vendors that provide gear to US drinking water, wastewater, and industrial water systems. The federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks. A new index, called Water Supply Chain Watch and published by exposure management firm Securin, however, found almost twice as many vulnerabilities as public records identified – including 20 exploited flaws that weren't even in the federal government's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. The security provider compared data on water-tech vendors with records from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the FBI, and WaterISAC, drawing on CISA advisory data through November 20 and KEV catalog entries through November 23. It found that federal water advisories hit their highest level this year since 2020. However, the volume of security alerts isn't a reliable predictor of real-world attacks, the researchers noted. Five vendors – Rockwell Automation (58), Advantech (48), Schneider Electric (35), Siemens (26), and ABB (24) – account for 191 of the 376 water-tagged security advisories. The No. 2 firm, Advantech, accounted for the highest number of vulnerabilities rated critical, but none of the CVEs in its advisories appear in CISA's KEV catalog. Unitronics, on the other hand, accounted for only two water-tagged security advisories, but at least 75 of its controllers were compromised between November 2023 and January 2024 by attackers taking advantage of default or missing passwords. The report also highlights another disconnect between water-related CVEs and real-world cyberattacks, which don't always require attackers to exploit software bugs. The July intrusions, which security researchers suspect were the work of Iran-linked attackers , targeted more than 100 water systems , with incidents reported across at least 12 states , and involved poorly secured internet-connected controllers . According to Securin, 791 Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers across multiple industries in the US were exposed to the internet as of November 17. Additionally, research by Forescout cited by the security shop found that most exposed Rockwell controllers in the US – seven in 10 – sit on mobile carrier networks, where poorly secured cellular modems can provide an entry point for attackers. item.content:encoded: American water systems are even less secure than we thought, according to a study of 236 technology vendors that provide gear to US drinking water, wastewater, and industrial water systems. The federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks. A new index, called Water Supply Chain Watch and published by exposure management firm Securin, however, found almost twice as many vulnerabilities as public records identified – including 20 exploited flaws that weren't even in the federal government's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. The security provider compared data on water-tech vendors with records from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the FBI, and WaterISAC, drawing on CISA advisory data through November 20 and KEV catalog entries through November 23. It found that federal water advisories hit their highest level this year since 2020. However, the volume of security alerts isn't a reliable predictor of real-world attacks, the researchers noted. Five vendors – Rockwell Automation (58), Advantech (48), Schneider Electric (35), Siemens (26), and ABB (24) – account for 191 of the 376 water-tagged security advisories. The No. 2 firm, Advantech, accounted for the highest number of vulnerabilities rated critical, but none of the CVEs in its advisories appear in CISA's KEV catalog. Unitronics, on the other hand, accounted for only two water-tagged security advisories, but at least 75 of its controllers were compromised between November 2023 and January 2024 by attackers taking advantage of default or missing passwords. The report also highlights another disconnect between water-related CVEs and real-world cyberattacks, which don't always require attackers to exploit software bugs. The July intrusions, which security researchers suspect were the work of Iran-linked attackers , targeted more than 100 water systems , with incidents reported across at least 12 states , and involved poorly secured internet-connected controllers . According to Securin, 791 Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers across multiple industries in the US were exposed to the internet as of November 17. Additionally, research by Forescout cited by the security shop found that most exposed Rockwell controllers in the US – seven in 10 – sit on mobile carrier networks, where poorly secured cellular modems can provide an entry point for attackers. A CISA advisory from July describes this technique: The authoring agencies observed Iranian-affiliated APT actors using several foreign-based IP addresses to access internet-facing PLCs manufactured by Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley, Schneider Electric, Siemens, and potentially other manufactured PLCs [ T0883 ]. The actors used leased, third-party hosted infrastructure and manufacturers’ PLC programming software to connect to misconfigured victim PLCs. Inbound malicious traffic has been observed targeting PLC devices on the following ports: 44818, 2222, 102, and 502, as well as targeting modems on port 22. These cellular modems, often installed by third-party contractors, frequently aren’t documented. Unsurprisingly, the top recommendation for water utilities is to find every cellular modem in the environment, including those installed by contractors, make sure they aren’t exposed to the open internet, and put a gateway with multifactor authentication (MFA) in front of them to stop would-be intruders from gaining access via the modem and controller combo. “Water utilities are spending time and money fixing the vulnerabilities they're told to worry about,” Securin CEO Srinivas Mukkamala said in a statement. “Meanwhile, attackers are getting in through equipment nobody knew was connected or passwords nobody bothered to change.” ®

item.title: NASA Enhances Supplier Program, Announces Mentor-Protégé Agreement
item.description: NASA’s Office of Small Business Programs (OSBP) hosted a ceremonial Mentor-Protégé Agreement signing between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace on Oct. 29, 2026, at the U.S. Space and Rocket Center in Huntsville, Alabama. Pictured in the front row, from left to right, are Pauline Sevigny, president and owner, GRACE Aerospace; Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager, The Boeing Company; and Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, OSBP. Pictured in the back row, from left to right, are Danielle Barnes, small business specialist, OSBP; Grant Crawford, Logan Ojermark, Nikki Howard, and Sabrina Pearson, contracting officers, NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) stages team; Christen Edwards, lead, SLS stages team; Bradley Niese, NASA’s senior procurement executive, deputy chief acquisition officer, and assistant administrator, Office of Procurement; Chris Hall, program manager, OSBP; and Kristina Parmenter, procurement officer, NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center. Credit: Justin Fields, Light Rain Studio How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA announced its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace. NASA is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program, as well as reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These improvements are aimed at making supplier development more accessible, efficient, and closely aligned with NASA’s mission needs. “We have intentionally redesigned the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success,” said Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator, Office of Small Business Programs, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “By simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on the capabilities NASA needs most, we are helping build a stronger, more resilient supplier base that can support the agency’s highest-priority missions.” Under the new Mentor-Protégé Agreement, Boeing will provide structured assistance to help GRACE expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, valued at nearly $500,000. “Boeing is proud to continue its longstanding relationship with NASA in support of its mission and the opportunities this agreement creates for Boeing, GRACE, and the broader aerospace industrial base,” said Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing. “Through this partnership, Boeing looks forward to sharing our expertise to support the continued growth and long-term success of a small business while strengthening our supplier base.”

item.title: Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location
item.description: A northern gannet ( Morus bassanus ) tagged with biologging devices on its back and tail Steve Votier Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track. Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage. In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite ‘blind spots’ also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU). Advertisement Read more Most large fishing boats go untracked as ‘dark vessels’ Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are only tracked “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”. The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets ( Morus bassanus ) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast. Overall, 12 per cent of the vessel detections made by the four critically endangered Balearic shearwaters ( Puffinus mauretanicus ) included in the study couldn’t be matched to public data. But given the high vessel density where they were – off the Catalan coast – the researchers estimated that up to 20 per cent of the vessels detected by the four birds weren’t broadcasting their identity. Tammy Davies at BirdLife International – a global partnership of non-governmental organisations – who wasn’t involved in the study, says the research could “give us a more complete picture of the risks seabirds face at sea” and “ultimately, this could contribute to better assessments of bycatch risk and help identify fisheries and areas where conservation measures are most needed”. Peter Ejbye-Ernst at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement (NSCR), describes the study as “fascinating” from a green criminology point of view, too. A tagged northern gannet coming in to land in Wales Steve Votier “What this study is somewhat proposing is that we can also look outside of humans for witnesses too,” he says, which overcomes a key barrier in observing crime at sea. item.content:encoded: A northern gannet ( Morus bassanus ) tagged with biologging devices on its back and tail Steve Votier Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track. Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage. In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite ‘blind spots’ also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU). Advertisement Read more Most large fishing boats go untracked as ‘dark vessels’ Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are only tracked “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”. The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets ( Morus bassanus ) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast. Overall, 12 per cent of the vessel detections made by the four critically endangered Balearic shearwaters ( Puffinus mauretanicus ) included in the study couldn’t be matched to public data. But given the high vessel density where they were – off the Catalan coast – the researchers estimated that up to 20 per cent of the vessels detected by the four birds weren’t broadcasting their identity. Tammy Davies at BirdLife International – a global partnership of non-governmental organisations – who wasn’t involved in the study, says the research could “give us a more complete picture of the risks seabirds face at sea” and “ultimately, this could contribute to better assessments of bycatch risk and help identify fisheries and areas where conservation measures are most needed”. Peter Ejbye-Ernst at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement (NSCR), describes the study as “fascinating” from a green criminology point of view, too. A tagged northern gannet coming in to land in Wales Steve Votier “What this study is somewhat proposing is that we can also look outside of humans for witnesses too,” he says, which overcomes a key barrier in observing crime at sea. In terms of its applications for cracking down on IUU, he says: “There’s a fine line between trying to understand something better and document it and then trying to control it and surveil it.” There are caveats, as the study has a small sample size and records both false-negatives and false-positives. It also gives very little information on the type of activity vessels were carrying out. But, while the research isn’t a solution to the problem of IUU, it is “part of the toolbox” for understanding what is happening at sea, says Ejbye-Ernst. The study didn’t differentiate between the size of vessels, but Rutter and his colleagues say this would be a good area for future research. Powerful images show dark side of South-East Asia’s fishing industry Photographer Nicole Tung captures the tough world facing South-East Asia’s fishers and their families in this series of images, which won her the Carmignac Photojournalism Award for fieldwork “Animal-borne audio recorders could potentially be used to investigate other ecological interactions and human activities that are difficult to observe directly, particularly in the marine environment,” says team member Ana Bertoldi Carneiro , also at BirdLife International. Hugo Tagholm at the charity Oceana says it is shocking that so many of the interactions were with unseen vessels, but he is concerned about attaching devices to seabirds on a broader scale to track this. “Seabirds are already grappling with the harm caused by overfishing and climate breakdown, we don’t want to put them at even greater risk from vessel operators acting illegally,” he says. “What we need is mandatory remote electronic monitoring across all fishing vessels, clear and effective laws and catch limits to protect and restore our seas, and truly deterrent sanctions for those breaking the law.” Journal Reference: Science Advances DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh2224

item.title: SpaceX Starship debris becomes art in Ashley Zelinskie's 'The Weight of Space' (video, photos)
item.description: null When a SpaceX Starship broke apart over Turks and Caicos in Jan. 2025, pieces of its heat shield washed ashore. Some of that material now hangs on a gallery wall in New York City, embedded in artist Ashley Zelinskie's print of the very explosion it survived. Look closely at the print and you can see little flakes on the surface. Some of Zelinskie's friends vacationing on the islands had come across pieces of heat-shield tile. "I think you might want these," Zelinskie recalled one friend telling her. She did. The Brooklyn-based artist ground the fragments into dust and worked them into the print. Ashley Zelinskie incorporated dust from recovered SpaceX Starship heat-shield tiles into this print of the vehicle breaking apart over Turks and Caicos. (Image credit: Ashley Zelinskie) The Starship print is part of "Ejecta," which captures rocket plumes and explosions on paper. It's one of four series in Zelinskie's solo exhibition, "The Weight of Space," which opened Nov. 20 at Heft Gallery in Manhattan. Her marble sculptures in "Monuments" depict the Hubble Space Telescope, retired NASA astronaut Mike Massimino's spaceflight gear and more. Five "Launch Sequence" sculptures follow a rocket through liftoff, and the interactive "Crowded Sky" lets visitors track what's currently orbiting overhead in real time. Zelinskie gave Space.com Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik and me a tour before the gallery doors opened. Massimino joined her that evening to celebrate the exhibition and their collaboration on "Monuments." You can watch the tour in the video above. Monuments Massimino turned up in our first look at Zelinskie's work, too. In 2022, I photographed the two of them beside her "Exploration JWST" sculpture at "Unfolding the Universe: First Light," an exhibit inspired by the James Webb Space Telescope's first images. Four years later, Massimino stood in a New York gallery looking at another Zelinskie sculpture. "That's my arm there," he told Malik. Artist Ashley Zelinskie and Space.com Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik discuss the sculpture between them, which depicts astronaut Mike Massimino’s bare hand gripping a replica of the handrail he pulled off the Hubble Space Telescope in 2009. (Image credit: Future/Steve Spaleta) In that hand is a piece of hardware Malik remembers watching Massimino wrestle with in real time. During NASA's final Hubble servicing mission in 2009, a stripped bolt left a handrail blocking access to the telescope's Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS). Mission Control instructed Massimino to forcibly remove the handrail so he and fellow spacewalker Michael Good could get on with the repair. Massimino told Malik that pulling the handrail off Hubble brought back a childhood memory of his father and his Uncle Frank driving a long screwdriver through a stuck oil filter. item.dc:creator: Steve Spaleta
item.content:encoded: null When a SpaceX Starship broke apart over Turks and Caicos in Jan. 2025, pieces of its heat shield washed ashore. Some of that material now hangs on a gallery wall in New York City, embedded in artist Ashley Zelinskie's print of the very explosion it survived. Look closely at the print and you can see little flakes on the surface. Some of Zelinskie's friends vacationing on the islands had come across pieces of heat-shield tile. "I think you might want these," Zelinskie recalled one friend telling her. She did. The Brooklyn-based artist ground the fragments into dust and worked them into the print. Ashley Zelinskie incorporated dust from recovered SpaceX Starship heat-shield tiles into this print of the vehicle breaking apart over Turks and Caicos. (Image credit: Ashley Zelinskie) The Starship print is part of "Ejecta," which captures rocket plumes and explosions on paper. It's one of four series in Zelinskie's solo exhibition, "The Weight of Space," which opened Nov. 20 at Heft Gallery in Manhattan. Her marble sculptures in "Monuments" depict the Hubble Space Telescope, retired NASA astronaut Mike Massimino's spaceflight gear and more. Five "Launch Sequence" sculptures follow a rocket through liftoff, and the interactive "Crowded Sky" lets visitors track what's currently orbiting overhead in real time. Zelinskie gave Space.com Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik and me a tour before the gallery doors opened. Massimino joined her that evening to celebrate the exhibition and their collaboration on "Monuments." You can watch the tour in the video above. Monuments Massimino turned up in our first look at Zelinskie's work, too. In 2022, I photographed the two of them beside her "Exploration JWST" sculpture at "Unfolding the Universe: First Light," an exhibit inspired by the James Webb Space Telescope's first images. Four years later, Massimino stood in a New York gallery looking at another Zelinskie sculpture. "That's my arm there," he told Malik. Artist Ashley Zelinskie and Space.com Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik discuss the sculpture between them, which depicts astronaut Mike Massimino’s bare hand gripping a replica of the handrail he pulled off the Hubble Space Telescope in 2009. (Image credit: Future/Steve Spaleta) In that hand is a piece of hardware Malik remembers watching Massimino wrestle with in real time. During NASA's final Hubble servicing mission in 2009, a stripped bolt left a handrail blocking access to the telescope's Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS). Mission Control instructed Massimino to forcibly remove the handrail so he and fellow spacewalker Michael Good could get on with the repair. Massimino told Malik that pulling the handrail off Hubble brought back a childhood memory of his father and his Uncle Frank driving a long screwdriver through a stuck oil filter. "Then my uncle Frank pulled to get more leverage, and that's what was going through my mind when I pulled off that handrail," Massimino said. He remembered looking down at Earth and thinking, "This one's for you, Uncle Frank." Massimino wore bulky, pressurized gloves to pull off the handrail, but Zelinskie chose to show his bare hand gripping the copper-plated replica. "I wanted to bring the humanity back into the piece," she told Malik. Ashley Zelinskie's marble sculptures of retired NASA astronaut Mike Massimino's gloves, reentry helmet and boots are part of her "Monuments" series at Heft Gallery in New York City. (Image credit: Ashley Zelinksie) The gloves have a story of their own. When Massimino brought a pair to her studio to be 3D-scanned, Zelinskie noticed how the fabric held its folds when the gloves were set down. "Oh my god, these want to be stone," she recalled thinking. So she went out and learned to work in marble. The astronaut boots have a detail you could easily miss from above. Zelinskie polished the soles smooth because, as she put it, "they're built for floating in space." For her sculpture of Massimino's reentry helmet, the kind he wore for the trip home from space, Zelinskie paired carved marble with a 3D-printed visor, which she electroplated and polished to a mirror finish. A veil carved from marble drapes over Zelinskie's Hubble Space Telescope sculpture, a nod to the blurry images Hubble first sent back to Earth. (Image credit: Steve Spaleta/Future) The Hubble Space Telescope gets its own marble tribute in "Monuments." Zelinskie started with a NASA 3D model of the telescope and used the modeling software Blender to give it a veil. "So I kind of threw a digital piece of fabric on the Hubble telescope over and over and over again until I got it right," she told Malik. The veil is a nod to the blurry images Hubble first sent back to Earth. A Digital Stone Project robotic arm in Tuscany carved the rough shape in marble, and Zelinskie finished it by hand. When she invited Malik to touch what looked like cloth, he reached out. "It's like a very buttery, smooth surface," he said. Ejecta The last time we saw Zelinskie at Heft, she and DJ and producer illich Mujica had filled the gallery with Webb imagery, live electronic music and a little Pink Floyd for their audiovisual performance "Redshift." We've also seen her turn Webb's view of the Pillars of Creation into artwork . This time, one of the images on the wall began with a camera Zelinskie pointed at a rocket herself. Zelinskie used a photograph she took at NASA's Artemis 2 launch to create this work in her "Ejecta" series. (Image credit: Ashley Zelinskie) Zelinskie photographed NASA's Artemis 2 launch from the Kennedy Space Center visitor center in Florida. The resulting print is part of "Ejecta," alongside the Starship breakup print and more. She uses data to distort the image until the swirls in a rocket plume start to resemble a nebula. Another print in the series depicts the loss of the space shuttle Challenger. That one has a personal connection for me. Jan. 28, 1986, was my birthday. Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff that day, killing all seven crew members. The memory of that day helped inspire my career covering space. Massimino spoke with Malik about what it was like to see a familiar image of the disaster through Zelinskie's eyes. "It's an artist's interpretation of it, which in some way, when I look at it, is more emotional," he said. Ashley Zelinskie's "Ejecta" series includes this print depicting the loss of NASA's Space Shuttle Challenger on Jan. 28, 1986. (Image credit: Ashley Zelinskie) Launch Sequence In "Launch Sequence," Zelinskie captures the changing shape of a rocket's exhaust cloud as the vehicle climbs away. (Image credit: Ashley Zelinksie) "I just became obsessed with launch clouds," Zelinskie told Malik. That fascination made its way into "Launch Sequence," a series of five sculptures that capture successive moments of liftoff. The cloud grows as the rocket climbs away. For the shape of the rocket itself, Zelinskie drew on sculptor Constantin Brâncuși's "Bird in Space" to give it the feeling of upward motion. Crowded Sky The tour ends with "Crowded Sky," where visitors can follow individual objects in Earth orbit. White markers represent government-owned objects and black markers represent privately owned ones. When the display picks out a target, scan a QR code and your phone tells you what you're looking at, what it does and when it launched. Wind the clock back far enough and there's just one object to follow. Run it a decade into the future and you get Zelinskie's projection of how much busier the sky could become. "Crowded Sky" lets gallery visitors follow an object in Earth orbit and discover who owns it, what it does and when it launched. (Image credit: Steve Spaleta/Future) With all those objects circling overhead, Malik asked Zelinskie what space means to her. "I think the more we learn about space, the more we appreciate our own planet," she said. "It's the overview effect. And I'm hoping that everybody gets that out of the artwor

item.title: Green light for Starmind: SpaceX gets approval to deploy 1 million AI satellites
item.description: null Earth orbit could get a lot more crowded in the coming years. The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) just granted SpaceX approval to deploy one million of its Starmind AI data-center satellites in orbit. "This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said today (Nov. 25) in a statement announcing the approval. AI has become central to SpaceX's business plans and identity over the past year or so. For example, the company has said that it's eyeing a "total addressable market" of $28.5 trillion over the long haul — and nearly $23 trillion of that is in "enterprise AI applications." Starmind is key to those lofty ambitions. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk believes that the future of AI compute is in space, where energy (from the sun ) is unlimited and there are no land-owning neighbors to lodge NIMBY complaints. SpaceX aims to launch the first of its Starmind satellites in the third quarter of 2027. The spacecraft will fly on the company's fully reusable Starship megarocket, which has deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink satellites on its most recent two test flights . Those 52 spacecraft are the vanguard of another enormous constellation: Musk has said that the next-gen Starlink network will eventually consists of about 100,000 satellites . The planned numbers for Starlink and Starmind are truly mind-boggling. To put them into perspective: Since the dawn of the space age in 1957, humanity has launched a total of just 28,000 satellites, give or take a few hundred. And the biggest constellation ever operated to date, the current iteration of Starlink, consists of about 11,000 spacecraft. These coming buildouts will require an enormous number of launches. Starship can carry a maximum of 60 V3 Starlink satellites per launch, for instance, so it will take about 1,700 liftoffs just to assemble that network (and more to maintain it, as the operational life of each satellite is expected to be about five years). Putting so many satellites into orbit also raises the risks of collisions. SpaceX has proven to be extremely proficient in this regard with its current Starlink satellites, which can detect and avoid potential collisions autonomously. But more evasive maneuvers will be required as space gets more and more crowded. SpaceX isn't the only company that aims to operate data centers in space; Cowboy Space , Starcloud, Blue Origin and Google, among other companies, have voiced similar ambitions. Starcloud and Google , in fact, have already launched AI pathfinder satellites. "Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America's leadership in SI," Carr said in the same statement. item.dc:creator: Mike Wall
item.content:encoded: null Earth orbit could get a lot more crowded in the coming years. The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) just granted SpaceX approval to deploy one million of its Starmind AI data-center satellites in orbit. "This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said today (Nov. 25) in a statement announcing the approval. AI has become central to SpaceX's business plans and identity over the past year or so. For example, the company has said that it's eyeing a "total addressable market" of $28.5 trillion over the long haul — and nearly $23 trillion of that is in "enterprise AI applications." Starmind is key to those lofty ambitions. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk believes that the future of AI compute is in space, where energy (from the sun ) is unlimited and there are no land-owning neighbors to lodge NIMBY complaints. SpaceX aims to launch the first of its Starmind satellites in the third quarter of 2027. The spacecraft will fly on the company's fully reusable Starship megarocket, which has deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink satellites on its most recent two test flights . Those 52 spacecraft are the vanguard of another enormous constellation: Musk has said that the next-gen Starlink network will eventually consists of about 100,000 satellites . The planned numbers for Starlink and Starmind are truly mind-boggling. To put them into perspective: Since the dawn of the space age in 1957, humanity has launched a total of just 28,000 satellites, give or take a few hundred. And the biggest constellation ever operated to date, the current iteration of Starlink, consists of about 11,000 spacecraft. These coming buildouts will require an enormous number of launches. Starship can carry a maximum of 60 V3 Starlink satellites per launch, for instance, so it will take about 1,700 liftoffs just to assemble that network (and more to maintain it, as the operational life of each satellite is expected to be about five years). Putting so many satellites into orbit also raises the risks of collisions. SpaceX has proven to be extremely proficient in this regard with its current Starlink satellites, which can detect and avoid potential collisions autonomously. But more evasive maneuvers will be required as space gets more and more crowded. SpaceX isn't the only company that aims to operate data centers in space; Cowboy Space , Starcloud, Blue Origin and Google, among other companies, have voiced similar ambitions. Starcloud and Google , in fact, have already launched AI pathfinder satellites. "Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America's leadership in SI," Carr said in the same statement. ("SI" stands for super intelligence, the Trump administration's preferred term for AI.) "By moving compute capacity beyond Earth , SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment," Carr added. "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home."

item.title: Backblaze explains why it's sharing customer information with advertisers
item.description: Some customers have raised concerns about Backblaze's privacy policy taking effect next month, which says the backup and cloud storage company may sell certain personal information to advertisers. Backblaze’s current privacy policy says that in addition to the personal information that users may provide, such as their email address when creating an account, it may also “automatically” collect information, such as “your software, the operating system you use when accessing our service, your Internet Protocol address, and the date and time of each request you make to Backblaze.” The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other company for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers. Read full article Comments

item.title: The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites
item.description: In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers. If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold. "The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement on Wednesday. "This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth." Read full article Comments

item.title: Huawei and crew tout homegrown EDA tools to overcome China’s fab deficit
item.description: Chinese telecom and IT giant Huawei boasted about its advancements in domestic electronic design automation (EDA) software this week, which it needs to accelerate the adoption of homegrown chip manufacturing. EDA is an umbrella term for software, hardware, and services essential to the planning, design, and production of modern chips. Today, Cadence Design Systems, Synopsys, and Siemens dominate the industry, but US export controls have restricted Huawei and other blacklisted Chinese businesses' access to their tools. The US blacklisted Huawei back in 2019 over concerns the telecommunications equipment giant could be forced to inject backdoors into its gear. Unable to access top EDA tools, Huawei’s chip division, HiSilicon, was forced to develop its own with the help of Phlexing Technology. This week, Phlexing chairman Qing He detailed the company’s efforts to bring new EDA tools to support Huawei’s so-called Tau Scaling Law design philosophy. “Tau EDA is the domestic EDA tool chain for Tau chips. It comes from a long, close partnership with Huawei,” he said. We discussed the tech earlier this year, but in a nutshell, it involves using advanced packaging, specifically 3D hybrid bonding, to achieve higher transistor density for a given area. The TSMC of China, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC), is still years behind Taiwan, South Korea, and the US on process technology. It currently has the ability to mass-produce chips on the equivalent of a 7 nm process. For comparison, TSMC began producing 5 nm-class products in 2020 and commenced mass production of 2 nm-class chips in late 2025. So, Huawei aims to use 3D packaging to close the gap, but for this to happen, it first needs tools capable of designing such chips, and that’s just what Phlexing claims to have done with its GloryBolt and GloryEX platforms. “Traditional EDA has long handled only single processes. Tau EDA needs to integrate and decompose multiple processes,” He said. “Coupling multi-scale, multi-structure, and multi-physics issues called for new analysis tools.” This, He says, culminated in the co-development of a process design kit (PDK) with Huawei beginning in 2024. These technologies have now gone live. The development comes as Huawei looks to bring larger, more capable processors to market. We previously discussed the company’s latest developments around AI accelerators, near packaged optics, networking, and rack systems. Many of these advancements will depend on multi-die chip packages, enabled by EDA tools, like those built by Phlexing. ®

item.title: AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it
item.description: MARK SYKES/SPL/Alamy There is a story, possibly apocryphal, that when the mathematician G. H. Hardy was about to undertake a dangerous sea voyage, he sent a postcard to a colleague declaring “I have solved the Riemann hypothesis”. Hardy, a staunch atheist, joked that this would prevent his ship from sinking, as God would never let him claim the credit for such a major result without revealing the details of his proof. Hardy would probably be both astonished and aghast that we now have what seems to be a proof of the Riemann hypothesis , a problem that has vexed mathematicians since the 19th century, but that no one yet understands it. The consensus among mathematicians is that the proof, produced with the aid of AI, will hold, but that it will take much more work to make it comprehensible to humans. However you feel about AI, this is a watershed moment, and one that demonstrates just how little we still understand about the capabilities of the technology. As recently as last month, leading mathematician Terence Tao speculated that AI would eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis, but that it may not happen before 2050. Now, some mathematicians are considering whether their hardest and most infamous remaining problems could be settled within months. In a year that has left mathematicians reeling, this may be the knock-out blow. Advertisement This is a watershed moment, and it shows just how little we understand about AI’s abilities For non-mathematicians, the fall of the Riemann hypothesis is harder to interpret. In the past year, AI has seen incredible advances in both maths and coding, but it is perhaps no coincidence that in these arenas, with nothing more than computer code, answers can swiftly be checked and iterated upon, allowing for rapid improvement. When it comes to other human endeavours though, from art to zoology, such verification is far harder, involving either the messy physical world, or unknowable human taste – or both. Whether this verification gap can be closed may become the biggest question of our age. Answers on a postcard, please. What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental? It has been called the hardest problem in mathematics, and now through a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, the Riemann hypothesis may have finally been solved

item.title: Our verdict on Dark Eden by Chris Beckett: ‘Holy cow. Chapter 44!’
item.description: The New Scientist Book Club read Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden in November Since starting the New Scientist Book Club in May 2023, I have aimed to vary our books as much as possible, moving between science fiction and popular science, older classics and the hottest new titles. Occasionally, though, I’m afraid I let the power go to my head and just choose one of my own personal favourites. That’s what I did in November, with Chris Beckett’s novel Dark Eden , a book I’ve loved ever since it won the Arthur C. Clarke award in 2013. Set on the planet Eden, a sunless world that drifts alone far outside the Milky Way, this follows the descendants of two astronauts who were marooned there over a century earlier. Now numbering 532 people, they tell each other stories of the world their ancestors came from, and struggle to survive on this dark, cold planet as they await the return of “one of those sky-boats with lights on them”. I think it is all wildly imaginative and original and exciting. So it was with some trepidation that I awaited the verdict of my fellow book club members on our Discord channel. I really wanted everyone else to love it, too! Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter It started well. “I managed not to stay up all night reading, but the temptation was definitely there – I am hooked,” wrote Dee55. Les was similarly gripped. “Started it? I’ve only gone and finished it, haven’t I? It really got me in, and I found it a fascinating exploration of social anthropology and linguistics in a very small, isolated population. And the world-building was fascinating, too – very different flora and fauna.” Advertisement Several other members also cited the strength of the world-building in Dark Eden . I also love the lanternflowers and woollybucks of this planet, and was fascinated to learn, in an essay Chris wrote for book club members, that, when creating a world for a story, he doesn’t “usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent”. I think he definitely succeeds in that here. In Dark Eden, I imagined how life might exist on a sunless planet Dark Eden, the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, takes place on a rogue planet outside the Milky Way. item.content:encoded: The New Scientist Book Club read Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden in November Since starting the New Scientist Book Club in May 2023, I have aimed to vary our books as much as possible, moving between science fiction and popular science, older classics and the hottest new titles. Occasionally, though, I’m afraid I let the power go to my head and just choose one of my own personal favourites. That’s what I did in November, with Chris Beckett’s novel Dark Eden , a book I’ve loved ever since it won the Arthur C. Clarke award in 2013. Set on the planet Eden, a sunless world that drifts alone far outside the Milky Way, this follows the descendants of two astronauts who were marooned there over a century earlier. Now numbering 532 people, they tell each other stories of the world their ancestors came from, and struggle to survive on this dark, cold planet as they await the return of “one of those sky-boats with lights on them”. I think it is all wildly imaginative and original and exciting. So it was with some trepidation that I awaited the verdict of my fellow book club members on our Discord channel. I really wanted everyone else to love it, too! Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter It started well. “I managed not to stay up all night reading, but the temptation was definitely there – I am hooked,” wrote Dee55. Les was similarly gripped. “Started it? I’ve only gone and finished it, haven’t I? It really got me in, and I found it a fascinating exploration of social anthropology and linguistics in a very small, isolated population. And the world-building was fascinating, too – very different flora and fauna.” Advertisement Several other members also cited the strength of the world-building in Dark Eden . I also love the lanternflowers and woollybucks of this planet, and was fascinated to learn, in an essay Chris wrote for book club members, that, when creating a world for a story, he doesn’t “usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent”. I think he definitely succeeds in that here. In Dark Eden, I imagined how life might exist on a sunless planet Dark Eden, the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, takes place on a rogue planet outside the Milky Way. Award-winning author Chris Beckett explains how he thought through the science behind this night world There were some excellent debates about the language these people have developed – they double up on words for emphasis, for example (“big big”; “cold cold”), use bastardised forms of our words (“Landing Veekle”; “leckytrickity”), and talk about Starry Swirl – the Milky Way they can see in their skies, a wonderfully evocative image. “I think Beckett has done something really clever here. He’s created a language that feels familiar enough to read naturally, but is sufficiently different to remind us that this is an entirely separate culture that has evolved in isolation,” wrote Maria. “I enjoyed some of the language. Tom’s dick and Harry’s for instance,” wrote Matthew – referring to an exclamation the characters use for emphasis. “It’s contagious… yesterday I found myself saying Wow, it’s hot hot!” added leasabp. Dee55 also admitted to adopting some Edenisms: “My favourite bit of the language is ‘newhairs’! I am already using this for teenagers, but only to myself at present.” The story’s protagonist is John Redlantern, a young man who decides there must be more to life than waiting for rescue around the Circle of Stones that marks the original astronauts’ landing point on Eden, and tries to spark an exodus from the Family’s small valley to explore the wider planet. John definitely drew some mixed opinions from readers. “Problem is, I don’t much like our ‘hero’, he’s not a very sympathetic character, more Sméagol than Bilbo,” wrote Matthew. I chatted to Chris in an interview for book club members, and he was certainly aware of this: “He’s an awkward cuss, John, isn’t he? He’s not a particularly nice person,” he told me – before embarking on an enlightening discussion about why he chose to write from various viewpoints, and how hard it was describing the world of Eden from the perspectives of people who have never been anywhere else. “The discipline of just writing it from within the story is if I’m trying to describe the world to readers, I can’t use metaphors and analogies that refer to anything that’s outside of Eden. And that was quite tricky to do.” Book club member Laura Akers, like others, said she “definitely enjoyed the story more when I realized that John, despite his own intentions, is not intended to be our ‘hero’”. Overall, I think the book club mostly really enjoyed Dark Eden – I particularly appreciated leasapb’s comment: “Holy cow. Chapter 44!!!”, as I think the ending is fabulous – but one issue that was raised by a few people was the amount the characters have sex with each other. Incestuous sex. “Certainly one of the odd things I found was the casual attitude to sex,” wrote Alan_P. Maria agreed. “I found the casual attitude towards sex quite unsettling too, particularly because the characters often seem almost childlike in their behaviour and understanding of the world, yet discuss sex so matter-of-factly. I honestly couldn’t bring myself to think too much about the incest!” And while Barbara Howe “loved the worldbuilding, and the story of John’s breakaway family’s trek to find a better place”, she found the “constant and highly unerotic sex… offputting”. But given that at least some members have gone on to read the sequels, I think this was largely a popular choice – and a welcome change from the Earthly dystopias which seem to be dominating the big new sci-fi novels out this autumn (I’m looking at you, Audrey Niffenegger and Emily St. John Mandel ).

item.title: Is The Time Traveler’s Wife the perfect audiobook to experience on shuffle?
item.description: Josie Ford Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more Reader Jenny Ozanne writes to tell us of a horrific incident that befell her partner. He had bought Audrey Niffenegger’s novel The Time Traveler’s Wife as a CD audiobook, to listen to on long car journeys. “After a while, he complained that the plot was completely impossible to follow,” writes Jenny. “It was only when I checked his player that I realized he had accidentally set the CD to ‘shuffle’. “ Advertisement Jenny raises two points, which Feedback heartily endorses: “I’m still not sure what’s more impressive: the story’s ability to survive total chronological chaos, or the fact that he listened to three random chapters before suspecting anything was wrong.” Feedback would suggest that The Time Traveler’s Wife might be the ideal novel to experience on shuffle, since the narrative is heavily non-linear. The main character hops uncontrollably back and forth through history. This led us to wonder: would any similarly chrono-displaced stories survive the experience of being played on shuffle, or even be improved by it? We wondered, for instance, about David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas . This has six stories set in different periods, including a future in which human clones are used as cheap labour, and a more distant future in which everything has gone a bit Mad Max . The stories are linked by characters in later timelines reading about the earlier ones, and by subtle coincidences. What would it be like on shuffle? However, after careful reflection, we realised there is only one correct answer to this, and that is Shane Carruth’s 2004 film Primer , which tells the story of two tech bros who invent a time machine in their garage. At first, they use it to go back in time and make money on the stock exchange, only to become caught up in an escalating web of betrayal and deception as they endlessly rewrite their lives. Primer is so overcomplicated, so mind-wreckingly confusing, that some poor soul once went so far as to draw a diagram trying to convey its timeline. Posted on Reddit by u/Clawz114, the diagram looks like a cross between a metro map and a flowchart of the inner workings of a chemical factory. It is therefore possible that playing the scenes in random order might actually cause the film to make more sense. The last refuge of the true gift scoundrel is, of course, the scented candle. This item might as well come with a note saying, “Sorry, I couldn’t think of anything”. Readers looking to step up their scented candle game may wish to investigate JD + Kate Industries , which is run by a pair of humour writers with a sideline in themed scented candles. Posted on Reddit by u/Clawz114, the diagram looks like a cross between a metro map and a flowchart of the inner workings of a chemical factory. It is therefore possible that playing the scenes in random order might actually cause the film to make more sense. The scent of success It’s that time of year when many of us are thinking, “Oh blimey, I need to buy everyone presents” and then having a meltdown when we can’t think of anything. The last refuge of the true gift scoundrel is, of course, the scented candle. This item might as well come with a note saying, “Sorry, I couldn’t think of anything”. Readers looking to step up their scented candle game may wish to investigate JD + Kate Industries , which is run by a pair of humour writers with a sideline in themed scented candles. They have taken these tedious items to new and different places. For instance, consider the Late Bronze Age Collapse scented candle, which “commemorates everyone’s favorite late 13th century [BC] widespread societal collapse”. Happily, it doesn’t smell of violence and decay, but rather of “burning cedar”, since “Lebanese cedar was a popular building material in the Late Bronze Age”. Those with more contemporary tastes may wish to consider the AI scented candle, which has a little sculpture of a data centre on the top, “surrounded by a post-apocalyptic, bombed-out city”. What does it smell of, you ask? “Diesel generator exhaust fumes”. Finally, those nostalgic for the headier days of space exploration might appreciate the Apollo 11 scented candle. Disappointingly, this doesn’t smell of moon dust, which, as we understand it, basically smells of burning because it reacts with oxygen on contact. Instead, its scent mimics “a certain powdered orange drink mix often associated with the space program, but that was not brought on Apollo 11. The astronauts brought a generic, grapefruit-flavored powdered drink mix instead, because they selfishly did not consider us and our desire to market candles.” Feedback has no idea if these candles are any good, but we enjoyed JD + Kate’s website a lot. By the letter Let us foray once again into the wonderful world of scientific acronyms. First, two reader claims that, for reasons that will become obvious, we cannot verify. Michael Berkson tells us: “As a solicitor my late wife was involved in development of insurance for doctors. The firm had to tell the client that they needed to choose a better name. Their original choice was Professional Indemnity Support Scheme.” Michael says the clients were open to replacing “scheme” with “service”, which helps not at all. Likewise, Jim Taylor asserts that he was once confronted with a military programme intended to ensure that spare parts would always be available for key equipment. It was called the Contractor Repair Advanced Provisioning System. Finally, a story we can confirm is true because we looked it up. Reader Geraldine Beare is an indexer, which is one of those jobs that we often forget about but would swiftly notice if it wasn’t done. “I am at present indexing a book on goats,” says Geraldine. Through this assignment she has learned the acronym “OMAGOD”, which she recommends saying “quickly, or perhaps in a vaguely Scottish accent”. It actually stands for ovine mouth and gum obscure disease. Got a story for Feedback? You can send stories to Feedback by email at feedback@newscientist.com . Please include your home address. This week’s and past Feedbacks can be seen on our website .

item.title: ‘Blade Runner 2099’ cast praise the incredible set designs that brought the sci-fi universe to life: ‘it was all so well-realized’ (interview)
item.description: null Prime Video’s " Blade Runner 2099 " has arrived with an 8-episode limited series revealing what the "Blade Runner" world looks like 50 years after the events of director Denis Villeneuve’s "Blade Runner 2049." The most obvious change in this depressing dystopia is that replicants are running the LA show after some unmentionable ecological disaster and humans are now the ones relegated to underclass citizens. Starring Michelle Yeoh as a replicant cop named Olwen whose life clock is running out and Hunter Schafer as Cora, a desperate human posing as a replicant blade runner, "Blade Runner 2099" unties these two in a mystery revolving around a rogue blade runner and a deadly secret that might cause their city to implode. We connected with three of the sci-fi show’s main co-stars, Matthew Needham ("House of the Dragon"), Lewis Gribben ("T2 Trainspotting") and Dimitri Abold ("Love Addicts") to hear more about working with creator/showrunner Silka Louisa, and immersing themselves in " Blade Runner 2099's " vivid futuristic worldbuilding. "For me it's a lot simpler than egos because he's such a goal-oriented person and all of his stuff has such a police procedural quality to it," Needham tells SPACE regarding his role as Yahya, an emotionless replicant who despises all humans. "It was really fun to just follow what Silka [Louisa] did. She wrote this great, really exciting mystery thriller, and I just got to play in that.” Matthew Needham and Hunter Schafer star in "Blade Runner 2099" (Image credit: Amazon Prime Video) Scottish actor Gribben portrays Cora's ailing younger brother Elias, who has compromised mobility and a rocky relationship with his overprotective sister. "I've played a few characters that were fairly vulnerable or insular," he notes. "Then seeing the journey of this character grow in strength and confidence and feel like becoming his own man was so compelling to me. It’s almost a relationship that falls apart between brother and sister, and that's fascinating to me because that’s such a cool dynamic you don’t always really see in television shows. That was quite interesting and made me want to try and be in it." (Image credit: Amazon Prime Video) As Bebeto, a doctor, veteran of the replicants vs. humans war, and a black-market dealer helping his species procure IDs and passports off-world, Abold enjoyed exploring the many facets of his character. "Much like Matthew and Lewis, for me it was the journey that Bebeto goes on," Abold adds. "Starting out as someone who’s so hopeful and has to try and scrape up the last dregs of hope as things start falling apart. Being subject to circumstances like that inherently make for an interesting story arc and story in general. Throwing myself into that, especially after how well Silka crafted the story and script, was something I was totally ready for." Lewis Gribben, Hunter Schafer and Dimitri Abold in "Blade Runner 2099" (Image credit: Prime Video) "Blade Runner 2099’s" sets and locations featu

"I've played a few characters that were fairly vulnerable or insular," he notes. "Then seeing the journey of this character grow in strength and confidence and feel like becoming his own man was so compelling to me. It’s almost a relationship that falls apart between brother and sister, and that's fascinating to me because that’s such a cool dynamic you don’t always really see in television shows. That was quite interesting and made me want to try and be in it." (Image credit: Amazon Prime Video) As Bebeto, a doctor, veteran of the replicants vs. humans war, and a black-market dealer helping his species procure IDs and passports off-world, Abold enjoyed exploring the many facets of his character. "Much like Matthew and Lewis, for me it was the journey that Bebeto goes on," Abold adds. Being subject to circumstances like that inherently make for an interesting story arc and story in general. Throwing myself into that, especially after how well Silka crafted the story and script, was something I was totally ready for." Lewis Gribben, Hunter Schafer and Dimitri Abold in "Blade Runner 2099" (Image credit: Prime Video) "Blade Runner 2099’s" sets and locations feature detailed production design that allowed the actors to experience a seamless transition into the complex shoot. "For me and Dimitri, our first day was in Bebeto’s apartment, and it was all so well-realized,” Gribben recalls. "You saw all the gadgets because obviously Bebeto was a bit of a tinkerer of a character and had lots of machinery and works and stuff. It took up about 70% of the acting, and we just had to come with compelling conviction. It made it so easy. When you audition for these things, you feel like you have to act more because you’re in a blue screen vacuum. But then you’re there, and it’s so visually well created like that, it made it so easy to be immersed in it." "Blade Runner 2099" is currently airing all 8 episodes exclusively on Prime Video. The Vespera Pro 2 is virtually identical to the first model apart from an upgraded interior. Harry Bennett / Future The touch power button glows red when turned on. Harry Bennett / Future The 50mm aperture remains the same but adds an upgraded optical design and internal light baffling. Harry Bennett / Future Separate filters are available for the Vespera Pro 2 and I would highly recommend the dual-band filter for nebula imaging. Harry Bennett / Future It's an impressive balance Vaonis have struck here between usability and premium astrophotography output. Prior to the pro-line of Vespera smart telescopes, I would have thought that this quality of astrophotography would require the highest levels of astronomy knowledge, alongside a pricey lineup of separate instruments. item.title: NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus
item.description: As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving. Strawberries (left) grown in the Space Life Sciences Lab’s controlled environment chamber. Cucumbers (center) and lemon basil (right) grown in a controlled environment chamber at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. NASA Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly important as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet. While space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A new investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions. Sweet space strawberries Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating. Researchers at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries. Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions. Delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation. But looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft. Before crops like cucumbers can be grown and eaten in space, they must undergo extensive testing. item.content:encoded: As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving. Strawberries (left) grown in the Space Life Sciences Lab’s controlled environment chamber. Cucumbers (center) and lemon basil (right) grown in a controlled environment chamber at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. NASA Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly important as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet. While space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A new investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions. Sweet space strawberries Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating. Researchers at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries. Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions. Delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation. But looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft. Cucumbers show promise Many crops have been grown in space, but none so far have come from the gourd family. Cucumbers could be the first. Before crops like cucumbers can be grown and eaten in space, they must undergo extensive testing. NASA-funded researchers recently evaluated cucumbers for their growth, yield, and nutrition under spaceflight conditions. The researchers found that while the plants showed some signs of enlarged leaves, they produced a steady stream of edible fruit, according to a study published in August in the journal HortScience. Offering a variety of crops, such as cucumbers, not only benefits astronauts’ diets and mental well-being, but it also increases plant biodiversity, which can improve the likelihood of crop success on long-duration missions. Spicing up spaceflight Herbs can spice up life in space, turning a bland meal into a bold one. Lemon basil, an edible herb with a citrus scent and taste, is making strides in testing at NASA Kennedy. Researchers report that lemon basil passed its preliminary round of space crop testing and successfully underwent seed sanitization, which is required before spaceflight to remove microorganisms from the seeds. Lemon basil’s next steps include assessing its growth in plant pillows, which can house plants aboard the space station. Menu fatigue can quickly become a problem for astronauts, but fresh herbs like lemon basil help transform packaged meals into something new and satisfying, supporting human health and performance in space. Biological & Physical Sciences Division NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

item.title: Pakistani astronaut becomes 1st international visitor to China's Tiangong space station (photos)
item.description: null For the first time ever, a foreign astronaut has set foot inside China's Tiangong space station. That pioneer is Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who arrived at Tiangong aboard the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft early this morning (Nov. 25). "The Chinese space station is always something to look forward to!" the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) wrote in an update today (in Mandarin; translation by Google). "China's 'Tiangong' welcomes partners from all over the world to visit!" Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces, is a payload specialist on Shenzhou-24. He found his way onto the mission thanks to a space-cooperation agreement that China signed with Pakistan in Islamabad in February 2025 . Ali and his two Shenzhou-24 crewmates — commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi — enjoyed a short and smooth ride to their orbital destination. They lifted off atop a Long March 2F rocket on Tuesday (Nov. 24) at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT on Nov. 25) and reached Tiangong a little over six hours later. Tang and Wu will live aboard the outpost for the usual six-month stint. Ali, however, will come home in just a week, hitching a ride with two of the three Shenzhou-23 astronauts, who arrived at Tiangong in May . Ali will be busy during his short space stay, conducting a set of joint Chinese-Pakistani experiments. "Four collaborative projects in biotechnology and materials are planned, with Ali also scheduled to conduct an in-orbit experiment involving photosynthetic cyanobacteria," The Times of India wrote today . The third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain on the station until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore set a Chinese record, becoming the first astronaut from his country to live in low Earth orbit for a full year. Astronauts from the Soviet Union/Russia and the United States have already blazed this long-duration trail. The global record for longest continuous space stay is 437 days, set by cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov aboard the Mir space station from January 1994 to March 1995. Another look at the Shenzhou-23 and Shenzhou-24 astronauts aboard Tiangong on Nov. 25, 2026. (Image credit: CMSA) Ali is not the first person from Pakistan ever to reach space, by the way. That distinction belongs to adventurer Namira Salim, who traveled to suborbital space on a tourism flight with Virgin Galactic in October 2023. Shenzhou-24 is the 12th crewed mission to Tiangong, a three-module, T-shaped outpost that China finished assembling in late 2022. Well, "finished" might not be the right term; China plans to expand Tiangong , which is currently about 20% as massive as the International Space Station .

item.description: The fifth edition of Entertainment Week Africa brought together filmmakers, musicians, designers, artists, tech founders, investors, mentors, policymakers and fans for six days of screenings, showcases, masterclasses and celebrations under the theme Five Years of Closing the Gap . People from 121 countries and territories applied to speak, attend or screen their work, and more than 19,000 people joined the programme in person and online, as EWA streamed its sessions live for the first time. Over the six days, more than 150 speakers led nearly 100 panels, masterclasses, workshops, roundtables and podcast sessions, while around 50 films were screened across the week. The celebrations began on Opening Night at the Livespot Entertarium, where guests were treated to an evening of music, fashion, film and comedy to mark five years of EWA. Sixteen emerging artists performed in front of a room of industry leaders, creatives and partners, and the night featured an exclusive 30-minute screening of University of Side Hustle, the first scripted feature film from Livespot Studios , written by Dami Elebe and executive produced by Deola Art Alade . By day, EbonyLife Place hosted a packed programme across seven tracks: Film & TV; Music; Fashion & Beauty; AI & Tech; Art & Animation; Live Events & Production; and Creative Enterprise. Nissi Ogulu led a masterclass on animation as Africa’s next big storytelling frontier, and From Lagos to Disney explored what it takes to bring African stories to global screens. Creators picked up practical tips in sessions with Victoire, Ifeoma Udeme and Canva. Other sessions tackled sync licensing, music funding, building Africa’s touring circuit and turning creative skills into businesses. The podcast stage kept the energy going with live recordings of CreativiTea and Crea8torium , which closed the final day. Fashion took over the Entertarium for The Runway Coterie, an evening of bold collections that ended with the announcement of the EWA Fashion Lab winners after a week-long programme with mentors. Hooked By Lade won first place with ₦2 million, Estaz took second place and ₦1 million, and Melira placed third, winning ₦500,000. Lush Hair styled the runway as the show’s hair sponsor. Next door, the EWA Art Floor invited guests into The Spaces Between Us , an exhibition that blended photography, painting, installation, archival work, fashion and live performance. Curated by Jumoke Sanwo and produced with Revolving Art Incubator (RAI) as it celebrated its tenth anniversary, the exhibition featured work by 21 Nigerian artists and seven fashion designers. In the EWA Sound Lab, producers and songwriters spent time creating alongside Banx & Ranx, the Grammy-nominated, Juno Award-winning duo whose credits include records for Sean Paul, Dua Lipa and Ella Eyre . Fashion took over the Entertarium for The Runway Coterie, an evening of bold collections that ended with the announcement of the EWA Fashion Lab winners after a week-long programme with mentors. Hooked By Lade won first place with ₦2 million, Estaz took second place and ₦1 million, and Melira placed third, winning ₦500,000. Lush Hair styled the runway as the show’s hair sponsor. In the EWA Sound Lab, producers and songwriters spent time creating alongside Banx & Ranx, the Grammy-nominated, Juno Award-winning duo whose credits include records for Sean Paul, Dua Lipa and Ella Eyre . Filmmakers also had a dedicated moment in the spotlight as the British Council’s Film Lab Africa 2 Lagos Showcase premiered new work from its cohort of Nigerian screenwriters and creative producers. The 2026 EWA Ambassadors, Qing Madi, Malik Afegbua, Juma Jux, Boubacar Jiba, Akin Faminu, Genoveva Umeh, Efa Iwara, Motolani Alake and Collins Sekaugo, represented the breadth of talent EWA brings together, from music and film to digital art, fashion and tech. “Five years ago, we set out to build a home for African creativity, a place where talent is celebrated and given what it needs to go further,” said Deola Art Alade, Founder and Convener of Entertainment Week Africa. “This year, watching emerging artists, designers and filmmakers take their moment on our stages, with people tuning in from around the world, reminded us why we do this. item.title: Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable
item.description: Note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault . After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it's an installable package with automatic updating. Ladybird is most notable for what it isn't: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google's Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird's rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. "The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork," project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday's announcement. "The browser around it is modest, but functional." Read full article Comments
