When Williams got into UI, he had a rather ambitious plan: become the Best Graduating Student in his faculty. Getting there would require more than good intentions. There were 5:30am wake-ups, difficult Statistics courses, friends who became unofficial tutors, a ChatGPT Pro subscription in 300 level, job offers he turned down and one Demography exam that kept him awake for 36 hours. University, as it turns out, came with quite a few plot twists. In this interview with BellaNaija, Williams takes us through the habits, people and decisions that shaped his academic journey. He also tells us whether he got that coveted top spot, what he learnt from the opportunities he put on hold, and what he would tell another student hoping to graduate with First-Class Honours. If that’s a goal you’re working towards, you may want to take notes. Literally or otherwise. Williams Alamu celebrates graduating with First-Class Honours in Statistics from the University of Ibadan. At what point did you realise you were chasing a record-breaking grade? Was it a goal from Day 1, or did it evolve? It was a goal from day one, actually. When I gained admission into the University of Ibadan, I already had my mind set on graduating as the Best Graduating Student in my faculty. I knew becoming the overall Best Graduating Student in the university would require an extraordinary amount of work, but I felt being the best in my faculty was something I wanted to work towards. And, of course, that would also mean graduating as the best student in my department. The motivation behind that goal goes back to shortly after secondary school, when my parents enrolled me in a Cambridge A-level programme. I went into it hoping to achieve three A-stars, but Chemistry was a major struggle. As the examinations approached, I became increasingly worried about my performance. I think I was more afraid of not meeting my own expectations than I was of the examination itself. The thought of getting a B or C frightened me so much that I eventually decided not to sit for the examinations. Williams Alamu seated in a University of Ibadan lecture hall before a test during his Statistics degree. When I eventually gained admission into the University of Ibadan, I didn’t want to repeat that experience. I saw university as an opportunity to approach things differently. Rather than allow the fear of falling short to determine what I attempted, I wanted to embrace the challenge and give it my best effort. That’s where the ambition to become the Best Graduating Student in my faculty came from. In the end, I didn’t graduate as the Best Graduating Student in my faculty or department, but I graduated with a First Class, and that’s something I’m genuinely happy about. It wasn’t exactly the outcome I had envisioned, but unlike my experience with Cambridge A-levels, I didn’t allow the fear of falling short to stop me from trying. I set a goal, gave it my best effort, and saw it through. For me, that alone was a significant part of my growth. Explain your systems. Beyond “reading hard,” what were the specific study techniques or daily schedules that kept you at the top? I think one of the most important things I did was try my best not to miss classes. I attended a public university, so there were always distractions, but I made a conscious effort to be present. I wouldn’t say I paid 100% attention in every class, but I realised there was value in simply being there. Sometimes, lecturers made important statements or gave hints that proved useful in examinations. I also started studying by the fourth week of each semester, after giving myself some time to settle in and enjoy school. I would go over what had been taught that week and revisit earlier topics whenever I needed more background knowledge. Whenever I struggled with a question or finally understood a difficult concept, I took notes so I could return to them during examinations rather than start figuring things out all over again. Handwritten probability and mathematical Statistics notes from Williams Alamu’s study sessions at the University of Ibadan. I also relied heavily on my friends and was never ashamed to ask questions when I didn’t understand something. I was fortunate to have classmates who were willing to help, including Lateef Basunu , Akinmusire Esther , Moyosoluwa Opesitian , Shukuroh Oladokun , Franklin David and Samuel Okoosi . Lateef, in particular, was incredibly patient and would spend as much time as necessary explaining difficult concepts to me. I also learnt that I assimilated information better in the morning. I’ve always been an early riser, usually awake by 5:30 a.m., so I preferred to sleep early rather than force myself to study through the night. I made an effort to plan my days around my priorities. Looking back, there wasn’t one extraordinary technique behind my academic performance. It was a combination of attending classes, studying early, taking notes, asking questions and understanding when I worked best. Williams Alamu combines virtual study sessions with printed Statistics notes during his undergraduate studies at the University of Ibadan. What did you have to sacrifice? Tell us about the social events, personal time, hobbies or even sleep you had to put aside to protect your CGPA. I think the biggest sacrifices I made were actually in my career. Outside academics, I’m a designer, working primarily in product design and web experiences. As I grew in the field, more opportunities started coming my way, including full-time and remote job offers. However, combining those responsibilities with my academic workload was difficult, especially because I had already set a goal for myself at university. I remember receiving an offer to join a company as its founding designer just as I was about to begin my final examinations. There was also another opportunity involving relocation abroad. Both were opportunities I genuinely wanted, but I had invested so much in my education that I didn’t want to compromise on the academic goal I had set for myself. I wouldn’t say I sacrificed much socially, as I’ve never been someone who attends a lot of parties. My hobbies were a different story. I enjoy video games, but I deliberately waited until after university to buy the Nintendo Switch I had always wanted because I knew it could become another distraction. Sleep was another thing I occasionally sacrificed during examinations. I remember staying awake for almost 36 hours while preparing for a Demography examination, and there were other nights when I studied until 2 or 3 a.m. Looking back, university was about deciding what deserved my attention at different points. I couldn’t give everything the same level of attention, and for those four years, my academics had to take priority. Williams Alamu takes a break during an overnight study session in his department at the University of Ibadan. How did you handle the toughest courses or departmental hurdles that usually break a student’s GPA? I’ve always believed that when you don’t understand something, there’s no point pretending otherwise. Whenever I struggled with a course or topic, I sought help from people who understood it better. One person who helped me tremendously was Lateef Basunu. I would visit him at his hostel for one-on-one tutorials, where he patiently explained difficult concepts and worked

item.title: European Commission confirms personal data stolen in AI-assisted cyberattack
item.description: The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected users directly. Speaking at a press briefing on Monday , Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm. The stolen data includes the names and email addresses of people outside the EU institutions, though the Commission has yet to figure out how many users are affected or whether other personal information was compromised. Public access to the platform has been disabled as a precaution. Despite confirming the theft, the Commission hasn't contacted affected individuals directly. Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday. "There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier said. The notice warns users that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The Commission is also advising users not to hand over personal information to anyone who contacts them claiming to be involved in EU Academy activities. The trouble with notifying users via the EU Academy website is that they've already been told not to come back until January. A separate notice says the platform will be offline from November 11 through January 14, 2027, while the Commission rebuilds it. When it reopens, users will have to register again, and any record of their previous coursework won't be transferred. The Register has asked the Commission whether the downtime and the requirement to create new accounts are connected to the cyberattack.A spokesperson didn't answer those points. The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), the watchdog responsible for policing EU institutions' handling of personal data. The EDPS told The Register that the Commission had notified it of the incident in stages, but declined to say whether it considered the Commission's approach to notifying affected users sufficient. "I can confirm that the EDPS has been informed and notified in phases by the European Commission," a spokesperson said. "Our colleagues remain in regular contact with EC services on the cyberattack and its implication. This is an ongoing case, so I cannot tell you more at this stage on the actions the EDPS might take as supervisory authority." The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday , almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22. item.content:encoded: The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected users directly. Speaking at a press briefing on Monday , Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm. The stolen data includes the names and email addresses of people outside the EU institutions, though the Commission has yet to figure out how many users are affected or whether other personal information was compromised. Public access to the platform has been disabled as a precaution. Despite confirming the theft, the Commission hasn't contacted affected individuals directly. Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday. "There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier said. The notice warns users that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The Commission is also advising users not to hand over personal information to anyone who contacts them claiming to be involved in EU Academy activities. The trouble with notifying users via the EU Academy website is that they've already been told not to come back until January. A separate notice says the platform will be offline from November 11 through January 14, 2027, while the Commission rebuilds it. When it reopens, users will have to register again, and any record of their previous coursework won't be transferred. The Register has asked the Commission whether the downtime and the requirement to create new accounts are connected to the cyberattack.A spokesperson didn't answer those points. The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), the watchdog responsible for policing EU institutions' handling of personal data. The EDPS told The Register that the Commission had notified it of the incident in stages, but declined to say whether it considered the Commission's approach to notifying affected users sufficient. "I can confirm that the EDPS has been informed and notified in phases by the European Commission," a spokesperson said. "Our colleagues remain in regular contact with EC services on the cyberattack and its implication. This is an ongoing case, so I cannot tell you more at this stage on the actions the EDPS might take as supervisory authority." The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday , almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22. Several internal applications were temporarily taken offline, and while most had since been restored, some remained unavailable at the time of Thursday's briefing. The Commission has confirmed the attackers used an AI-assisted hacking tool, and the incident comes amid mounting concerns over ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework that security researchers have linked to large-scale cyber espionage campaigns. More than a month after the Commission first spotted the intrusion, Regnier was unwilling to say on Monday whether its security teams had finally seen off the hackers. "As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage on where we are," he said. ®

item.title: My Experience at the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos
item.description: The Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop, held in Lagos on 17 and 18 November 2026. When I got the email that I was selected for the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos, I knew, without doubt, that the cohort of writers I would engage with would be some of the finest around. I was not disappointed. The workshop put me in the same room with extremely talented writers I had read and admired from a distance. Some of us have shared publication credits and honours on longlists and shortlists of literary prizes over the past couple of years. For two days, we were guests of the British Council and students at the feet of our primary facilitator, Nigerian writer, journalist, and editor, Molara Wood . Liberian-American writer Wayétu Moore also facilitated a session, and a publishing masterclass was held by Anwuli Ojogwu and Eghosa Imasuen of Narrative Landscape Press. The twelve selected writers for the workshop are Azeeza Adeowu, Chinenye Okechukwu, Ahmad Adedimeji Amobi, Chinonso Nzeh, Innocent Chizaram Ilo, Kingsley Alumona, Mayowa Fagbure, Mustapha Enesi, Oluwatobi Afolabi, Súnmisọ́lá Olúdé, Ufuoma Bakporhe, and Winifred Odunoku. A combination of writers who are also journalists, editors, filmmakers, among other things. “Gotta Whack That Guy!” I first encountered Molara Wood on social media, where she shared her commentary on a plethora of issues, from literature and culture to politics. So I particularly looked forward to learning from her. On the first day, when I walked into the workshop at the British Council, she was there, standing and already conversing with the writers present. By the time other writers arrived and the round of introductions began, it illuminated the sort of people I was in the room with. I had read the writing samples and excerpts recommended for reading ahead of the workshop. They were really good. These writers seemed assured in their craft, and it became further obvious as the conversations became robust. Molara Wood, with all her brilliance, struck me even more with the animated manner in which she facilitated the workshop. As though she was more excited to teach than we were to be taught by her. This made the workshop flow seamlessly from the jump. We shared opinions on the assigned short stories. We discussed how well they used dialogue, descriptions, and language to reveal so much about the characters and the world they inhabit. item.content:encoded: The Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop, held in Lagos on 17 and 18 November 2026. When I got the email that I was selected for the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos, I knew, without doubt, that the cohort of writers I would engage with would be some of the finest around. I was not disappointed. The workshop put me in the same room with extremely talented writers I had read and admired from a distance. Some of us have shared publication credits and honours on longlists and shortlists of literary prizes over the past couple of years. For two days, we were guests of the British Council and students at the feet of our primary facilitator, Nigerian writer, journalist, and editor, Molara Wood . Liberian-American writer Wayétu Moore also facilitated a session, and a publishing masterclass was held by Anwuli Ojogwu and Eghosa Imasuen of Narrative Landscape Press. The twelve selected writers for the workshop are Azeeza Adeowu, Chinenye Okechukwu, Ahmad Adedimeji Amobi, Chinonso Nzeh, Innocent Chizaram Ilo, Kingsley Alumona, Mayowa Fagbure, Mustapha Enesi, Oluwatobi Afolabi, Súnmisọ́lá Olúdé, Ufuoma Bakporhe, and Winifred Odunoku. A combination of writers who are also journalists, editors, filmmakers, among other things. “Gotta Whack That Guy!” I first encountered Molara Wood on social media, where she shared her commentary on a plethora of issues, from literature and culture to politics. So I particularly looked forward to learning from her. On the first day, when I walked into the workshop at the British Council, she was there, standing and already conversing with the writers present. By the time other writers arrived and the round of introductions began, it illuminated the sort of people I was in the room with. I had read the writing samples and excerpts recommended for reading ahead of the workshop. They were really good. These writers seemed assured in their craft, and it became further obvious as the conversations became robust. Molara Wood, with all her brilliance, struck me even more with the animated manner in which she facilitated the workshop. As though she was more excited to teach than we were to be taught by her. This made the workshop flow seamlessly from the jump. We shared opinions on the assigned short stories. We discussed how well they used dialogue, descriptions, and language to reveal so much about the characters and the world they inhabit. We discussed how words, accents, and other idiosyncrasies of characters can reveal class, age and societal standing. This is why it is important for writers to observe the world. To observe the minute details of what makes up people, because these are the tools through which subtext can be created. The arts are connected, especially through the basic principles of storytelling. Molara Wood recognised this by using the context of films, mostly classics, to highlight storytelling techniques for better understanding. We discussed the dangers of anachronism in contemporary fiction through the critique of a Nigerian novel and the anachronistic elements therein. She hammered on the importance of reading widely, beyond the mainstream, beyond the contemporary, across literary cultures and traditions. We must read widely so we can know exactly what we are writing in response to. The workshop’s goal is in its name. The rudiments of writing are well known to writers, but not so much those of editing. To polish a story to the best it can be. “ To develop the inner practice of being attentive to define and understand the times ” . Editing one’s own work can be difficult. The sentimental value we place on our words makes it hard to, as they say, “kill your darlings”, but it is a necessity for the beauty of a story to shine through. For the writing to be better, we simply “Gotta whack that guy!” as Molara Wood called out from her workshop material. The afternoon session was facilitated by the Liberian-American novelist, Wayétu Moore. Her session was on Speculative fiction/Magical Realism. Naturally, the question raised is the extent to which these categorisations apply to the works of those who write from cultures where the material and the mystical spheres are considered to be in constant interaction. Such that the happenings that seem magical to a Western mind are random stories one hears from neighbours, friends and family so often that they are as real as anything, and an immutable fact. Tales of cats that bring down house walls, of children who die and return again and again, of grandfathers who come back as babies, of birds dropping from the sky and transforming into old women. Wayétu Moore was in conversation with us about this. The most important eye-opener for me during this session was about plot and character building. The rules for writing nuanced characters are the same regardless of whether a story is speculative or realist. Writers tend to venerate certain characters as saints and demonise others with no redeemable qualities, such that they are a clear antithesis of the other. But human beings are not that way. A supposedly evil character can be a loving husband. A torturer can be a caring father when he returns home every night. This is the nature of humans, the nature of the characters we want to portray in stories. It has been said that reality doesn’t necessarily make sense, but fiction should. The Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop, held in Lagos on 17 and 18 November 2026. “Forget technique… Write from here.” We all had one question on our tongues on the second day of the workshop: who wrote the assigned anonymised short story we were to discuss? It was a shocking story, quality-wise, and was written by one of the greats of 20th-century African Writing, we came to find out. A story that meanders and pulls up new surprises with every line. In a workshop with a focus on editing, it was the perfect case study for our facilitator to have us note not only its obvious flaws, but also its strengths. We learned even more about dialogue and voice, structural and contextual editing. The field was covered. Molara Wood wanted to get as much as possible done despite the short time we had together for the workshop. So we had to eat into our lunch breaks, quite literally. No complaints; there was so much to converse about. The sessions were interactive. We discussed each other’s writing samples, and then our works-in-progress in pairs, giving feedback on what we thought worked well, what didn’t. A way of putting into practice what we had spent hours learning during the workshop. One that was soon reaching its end. When Eghosa Imasuen and Anwuli Ojogwu of Narrative Landscape Press filled the room with their presence for the afternoon session, I knew it was going to be enjoyable. Eghosa Imasuen is a very jovial man, mixing English with Pidgin to land a point and make jokes. It felt as if he knew us all beforehand. The publishing industry in Nigeria has always fascinated me. What are contracts like? How well do books sell? These things are often shrouded in mystery. Eghosa spearheaded the session. Anwuli made her points where she thought necessary. Understanding the publishing process within a Nigerian publishing house like NLP was necessary for writers who, after fine-tuning stories or a novel, would seek out publishers. The session included tips on how to put together a publisher’s query for a manuscript, and the fine margins that can make a query sound professional and confident. “Be simple. Less is more,” Anwuli noted. You write a good story, rewrite, revise, edit, put together a pack of publishers’ queries and send it off with a hail of prayers. “Writers are the suppliers of stories,” Eghosa Imasuen explained. Publishers produce and sell them. It is looking at stories in the business sense, because publishing is a business, a precarious, courageous one. This was further highlighted when we got into the numbers of it all, information that I was glad to be privy to. The nature of p

item.title: The Beatz Awards 2026: Soso Soberekon Honoured with Special Recognition Award as May D and Shiiro Light Up 11th Edition
item.description: The 11th edition of The Beatz Awards, held on Saturday, November 21, 2026, at the Shell Hall, MUSON Centre, Onikan, Lagos, was a remarkable celebration of music, creativity, excellence and the exceptional talents working behind the scenes of the Nigerian music industry. Under the theme “Behind the Beat, Beyond the Beat,” this year’s ceremony brought together music professionals, industry stakeholders, producers, songwriters, DJs, engineers, media personalities and other key players to celebrate the creative minds whose contributions continue to shape the sound and business of African music. Soso Soberekon Receives Special Recognition Award One of the major highlights of the evening was the presentation of the Special Recognition Award to renowned music executive and industry figure, Soso Soberekon, in recognition of his remarkable contributions to the Nigerian music industry. From talent discovery and artist development to music promotion, business development and industry connections, Soso Soberekon’s influence and commitment to the growth of Nigerian entertainment continue to resonate across different sectors of the culture. The special recognition celebrates his role in creating opportunities, supporting talents and contributing to the development of the Nigerian music ecosystem. May D and Shiiro Deliver Electrifying Performances The ceremony also featured captivating musical performances, with award-winning singer May D delivering an electrifying performance that got the audience on their feet, while producer and songwriter Shiiro equally thrilled guests with an impressive performance, showcasing the creativity and musical excellence that The Beatz Awards continues to celebrate. Beatz to Banger Producers’ Challenge: Kevwe Praise Emerges Winner Another major highlight of the 11th edition was the highly anticipated Beatz to Banger Producers’ Challenge, an initiative designed to discover, nurture and provide opportunities for emerging music producers. The competition provided a platform for talented producers who participated in the Beatz to Banger 2.0 training programme to showcase their creativity, technical abilities and music production skills before an audience of industry professionals. Following an intense competition among the final five contestants, Kevwe Praise emerged as the ultimate winner, earning the coveted title and a cash prize of ₦1.5 million. The winner’s cash cheque was presented by Princess Damilola Sonayon-James , APC Deputy Governorship Aspirant, alongside the Chief Executive Officer of The Beatz Awards, Elijah John . The moment marked a significant milestone for the winning producer and reinforced The Beatz Awards’ commitment to creating tangible opportunities for emerging talents beyond recognition and celebration. Through the Beatz to Banger initiative, the platform continues to bridge the gap between music education, talent discovery and industry opportunities, empowering the next generation of music producers to move

item.title: BepiColombo takes the long way around Mercury after software glitch
item.description: A software fault cut short BepiColombo's Mercury orbit insertion burn, but the European Space Agency (ESA) says the mission remains on track to separate its two science orbiters on December 9. ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), still carrying JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), fired its four axial thrusters on November 21 to place the spacecraft in orbit. The burn began at 1824 UTC, when BepiColombo was approximately 635 km above the planet's surface. It was supposed to last for 37 minutes but shut down early . The shutdown , caused by a software issue involving attitude guidance and thruster control, left the spacecraft in safe mode, a protective state in which all non-essential activities cease. Ignacio Tanco, ESA's BepiColombo Flight Operations Director, said: "Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened." The burn achieved around 77 percent of the planned velocity change, securing an orbit around Mercury but leaving BepiColombo taking 75 hours to circle the planet instead of the intended 58. The good news is that multiple burns were always going to be needed to adjust the orbit ahead of Mio separation and MPO reaching its science orbit. "The remaining MOI [Mercury Orbit Insertion] sequence has already been adapted to the new trajectory, with no additional burns required," ESA said. "After each burn, the Flight Dynamics team determines the achieved orbit to then design the next manoeuvre," said Frank Budnik, ESA's BepiColombo Flight Dynamics Manager. "So, the sequence is not only more propellant-efficient, it also allows Flight Dynamics to adapt each subsequent burn to the spacecraft's actual trajectory. It's a dynamic sequence! Each new manoeuvre is based on the previous ones." Teams at ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) and Airbus continue to investigate the underlying software fault. ESA has not said whether the revised burn sequence will affect propellant reserves available for a possible mission extension. The separation of Mio and MPO is planned for December 9, and more burns will be needed to guide MPO to its final orbit by March 2027, with science operations starting in April 2027. ®

item.title: Man Theft Auto – why did so few women review GTA VI, the biggest video game of the decade?
item.description: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. Continue reading...

item.title: November's full moon rises tonight! Here's how to see the Beaver Moon supermoon
item.description: null Editor's Note: The November full supermoon dazzled stargazers with a spectacular show overnight on Nov. 24. Check out our photo wrap article to see spectacular images of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world. Get ready stargazers! The full "Beaver supermoon" rises in the eastern sky, offering up a spectacular display shortly after sunset tonight (Nov. 24). Here's what you need to know. November's full moon occurs at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk passes opposite the sun in our sky, making it appear fully lit from our perspective. The November full moon is often referred to as the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the small mammals are hard at work building their lodges in preparation for the winter. Viewers in the U.S. can even get a detailed look at the full moon ahead of local moonrise thanks to a free supermoon livestream from the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP), starting at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) today. The stream will feature live views of the lunar disk captured from the VTP's robotic telescopes in Manciano, Italy, weather permitting. The Beaver Moon is also set to be a dazzling supermoon , because it turns full as the natural satellite passes within 90% of perigee , when it is at its closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit. A supermoon's proximity can make it appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than the most distant full moon of the year, which is colloquially known as a "micro-moon". When to see the Beaver Moon November's full moon will be below the horizon for stargazers in the U.S. at the moment it turns full. Instead, viewers in America should look out for the moon shortly after sunset on Nov. 24, as it looms low over the eastern horizon. A supermoon can make for a spectacular sight when caught close to the horizon. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Try covering the lunar disk with your thumb to block out the worst of its glare, and you may just be able to spot to blue-white lights of the Pleiades open star cluster glimmering less than 10 degrees away — roughly the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length. If you miss the full moon on Nov. 24, don't worry as the moon will appear full to the casual observer for a couple more nights, so there's no excuse to miss it! Remember to check out Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location. What should I expect from the November supermoon? You may see the moon turn a striking orange-yellow hue as it rises because sunlight reflected from its disk passes through more of Earth's atmosphere, which scatters shorter bluer wavelengths of light and allows more red and orange light to reach our eyes in a process called Rayleigh scattering. Celestron Nexstar 4SE (Image credit: Celestron) This is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you quickly find a steady view of the moon. item.title: Temi Nkem’s Oversized Braided Updo Is the Hairstyle Inspiration We Needed
item.description: Big Brother Naija 2026 winner Temi Nkem pairs a structured matte-gold leather corset and black velvet skirt with an architectural braided updo. If your next braid appointment has you thinking beyond the usual ponytail or bun, Temi Nkem has an idea you might want to take to your hairstylist. The Big Brother Naija 2026 winner wore her thick braids in a high, sculptural updo, with oversized loops arranged into a crown. She paired it with a gold-and-black look, complete with metallic beauty details and contrasting textures. Rather than letting her thick braids fall down her back, Temi has gathered them into a sleek, high updo, building them into an oversized crown of interlocking loops. The result is sculptural, full of volume and beautifully structured. It’s also a great example of how to style thick braids when you want a fresh way to wear them for an event. Pulling the hair up keeps the face open, while the loops create plenty of interest around the crown. And with the base kept sleek, the hairstyle gets to take centre stage without feeling too busy. Temi Nkem accents her sleek looped braid updo with metallic gold-leaf detailing, brow crystal, and glossy nude lips. Then there are the beauty details. Temi goes for smoky brown eyeshadow, full lashes and a glossy nude lip outlined in brown, keeping the makeup warm and complementary to the outfit. A little gold takes things further: there’s a tiny cross-shaped crystal between her brows, three vertical micro-beads on her chin, hammered circular gold earrings and flecks of metallic gold leaf tracing the side of her face, from her left temple down to her collarbone. It’s an unexpected beauty detail, and one that ties in beautifully with the colours of her outfit. Temi Nkem shows how to style thick braids into a sculptural crown paired with a gold-and-black corset gown. Now, about that gown! Temi shows how to wear gold and black with ease, starting with a structured matte-gold leather corset bodice. It features vertical seam boning, a deep V-plunge neckline and a sharply defined V-shaped basque waist. Below it, a fitted black velvet skirt brings a different texture into the look, while matching off-the-shoulder velvet arm bands complete the silhouette. The contrast between the gold leather and plush black velvet is what makes the combination work so well. Rather than having both colours compete for attention, the matte gold adds warmth and the black velvet gives the outfit balance. So, if thick braids are next on your salon mood board, you might want to save Temi’s updo. And if you’re planning a gold-and-black outfit, her mix of leather and velvet is another styling idea worth keeping. item.title: InferNode gives Bell Labs' Inferno OS a 64-bit second wind
item.description: InferNode brings a modernized, 64-bit edition of Inferno, the distributed operating system that followed Plan 9 from Bell Labs. For us, the strapline of the InferNode project distracts from the interesting part. It describes the project as a "Secure Runtime for AI Agents," but we think it's something far more interesting than another LLM tool. Fair warning: this vulture has no interest whatsoever in AI agents, and we are not even going to look at this planned use of InferNode. We're interested in the OS, and here, its GitHub repository spells out the part that caught our attention: "a 64-bit Inferno® OS." That grabbed us because Inferno is a very interesting OS, although it doesn't get much attention – for example, the official Inferno GitHub repository shows little activity in the last few years. Inferno is the successor to Plan 9, which we've written and talked about before , including recent releases of its community continuation, 9front . Plan 9 is what the team who invented Unix did next. Plan 9 is a very minimalist, natively clustered Unix: machines can freely mount one another's filesystems, display windows on one another, and start processes on one another. Plan 9 turns a network of machines running this Unix-like OS into a single machine. So, for instance, if you were working on a laptop with limited storage and compute power, you could compile a large complex project on a faster machine elsewhere on the network, using project files located on a third machine, while watching the process in your terminal on your screen, with no messing about with SSH sessions. Plan 9 and 9front programs are compiled into architecture-specific native binaries. Different processor families can still work together across the network, but the same executable won't run unchanged on both an x86-64 laptop and an Arm64 server. Inferno takes a different approach. It's contemporaneous with the far less ambitious Java. On Inferno, languages compile code for a VM called Dis, which is part of the kernel. This means that Inferno binaries execute directly on anything that the Inferno kernel runs on. The OS kernel is built to run bare-metal, or as a process on various other OSes, without needing a separate hardware virtual machine or hypervisor. A single binary can run on all supported CPU architectures. Inferno applications are normally written in the Limbo programming language , whose documentation was written by Unix co-creator Dennis Ritchie. Limbo is one of the languages that influenced Go, but Inferno lets compilers for other languages target Dis as well. The binaries run anywhere. Inferno on Arm, or x86, or RISC-V, or running in a Windows or Linux or macOS process, your program just runs. We've been trying to contact Vita Nuova , the company that maintains Inferno, for some years without success. Development appears to have slowed considerably. item.dc:creator: Liam Proven
item.content:encoded: InferNode brings a modernized, 64-bit edition of Inferno, the distributed operating system that followed Plan 9 from Bell Labs. For us, the strapline of the InferNode project distracts from the interesting part. It describes the project as a "Secure Runtime for AI Agents," but we think it's something far more interesting than another LLM tool. Fair warning: this vulture has no interest whatsoever in AI agents, and we are not even going to look at this planned use of InferNode. We're interested in the OS, and here, its GitHub repository spells out the part that caught our attention: "a 64-bit Inferno® OS." That grabbed us because Inferno is a very interesting OS, although it doesn't get much attention – for example, the official Inferno GitHub repository shows little activity in the last few years. Inferno is the successor to Plan 9, which we've written and talked about before , including recent releases of its community continuation, 9front . Plan 9 is what the team who invented Unix did next. Plan 9 is a very minimalist, natively clustered Unix: machines can freely mount one another's filesystems, display windows on one another, and start processes on one another. Plan 9 turns a network of machines running this Unix-like OS into a single machine. So, for instance, if you were working on a laptop with limited storage and compute power, you could compile a large complex project on a faster machine elsewhere on the network, using project files located on a third machine, while watching the process in your terminal on your screen, with no messing about with SSH sessions. Plan 9 and 9front programs are compiled into architecture-specific native binaries. Different processor families can still work together across the network, but the same executable won't run unchanged on both an x86-64 laptop and an Arm64 server. Inferno takes a different approach. It's contemporaneous with the far less ambitious Java. On Inferno, languages compile code for a VM called Dis, which is part of the kernel. This means that Inferno binaries execute directly on anything that the Inferno kernel runs on. The OS kernel is built to run bare-metal, or as a process on various other OSes, without needing a separate hardware virtual machine or hypervisor. A single binary can run on all supported CPU architectures. Inferno applications are normally written in the Limbo programming language , whose documentation was written by Unix co-creator Dennis Ritchie. Limbo is one of the languages that influenced Go, but Inferno lets compilers for other languages target Dis as well. The binaries run anywhere. Inferno on Arm, or x86, or RISC-V, or running in a Windows or Linux or macOS process, your program just runs. We've been trying to contact Vita Nuova , the company that maintains Inferno, for some years without success. Development appears to have slowed considerably. Moving the runtime to 64-bit also raises compatibility questions: some forks change Dis's word size and cannot run existing 32-bit bytecode unchanged. We're aware of several efforts to build 64-bit versions of Inferno. Caerwyn Jones's Inferno64 is one of the more visible, and the GitHub repository (and indeed his X account ) show considerable activity. However, Inferno64's Dis is not compatible with 32-bit Dis code. Another fork is Dinsmoor's Inferno64 , which also shows recent activity, albeit with the assistance of the Claude LLM. Others include the long-quiescent Purgatorio and 9ferno , both inactive for years, plus Scott Guyon's more active fork . Dropping the compatibility goal altogether, Node9 replaces Limbo with Lua and Dis with LuaJIT . There are more forks and variants than we've gone into here. Given that there have been quite a few efforts, and most haven't delivered final ready-to-use products yet, we were surprised when InferNode was suddenly announced on the Inferno-OS mailing list last week. Developer Peter Finn said: "An experimental runtime for containing generative AI agents was the original motivation, but most of the work since has been on the OS itself, and the AI parts are ordinary file servers. For example, llmsrv at /mnt/llm and speech9p are started from the login profile, and if you delete those lines they're simply not there. There's also non-generative AI additions on object detection served as files at /mnt/vision, on the CPU or a GPU host, and voice calls between devices done by mounting each other's audio files over 9P. There's a GUI layer intended to facilitate hands-free AI agent use, but it too is optional." He also said that InferNode's development was largely independent of the existing efforts, partly because the primary target was Arm64, not x86-64. Its 64-bit Dis runtime is incompatible with the 32-bit original: "The opcodes, file format and magic number are unchanged, but the word size isn't, so frame sizes, offsets and pointer maps all differ. Limbo source recompiles without edits. A 32-bit .dis is currently rejected at load time." InferNode doesn't implement 9front's DP9IK authentication protocol , so it cannot connect to servers requiring that authentication. Dr Finn told us: "DP9IK is not quantum-safe. That's the reason. InferNode's current crypto policy is strict CNSA ." InferNode also includes some slightly unexpected components, related to its intended use for testing LLM agents – such as a wallet for the Ethereum cryptocurrency, which Finn said was "mainly to support agent payments." The first release of Inferno was in 1996, the year after Java and the JVM were launched. Inferno is a much more ambitious project, but its core function – the ability to run identical binaries on multiple platforms, without recompilation – was close enough that they ended up competing in the market, and Java won. It was a pleasant surprise to see a modernized version of Inferno arrive this year, 30 years on. Finn told us: "About a year ago I saw the potential for a 'break-out' moment for this tech as a runtime for containing AI agents. The flood of cybersecurity risks we would face on account of adversarial AI agents required new systems with small footprints and minimal attack surfaces. Inferno was a perfect candidate and it was an opportunity to show the world how visionary Plan 9's ideas were and how well they mapped on to pressing contemporary security issues." "If InferNode succeeds, it is an opportunity for Plan 9's ideas to migrate out of hobby-land and really make an impact – as they deservedly should." He has a point. On a related note, this vulture discussed the possibility of rebuilding the world's IT systems from scratch on last week's Kettle podcast . Perhaps the hour for tools like this really has come round at last. ®

item.title: Enoch Adeagbo Was Denied Admission for Being Too Young. At 19, He’s Set to Graduate with First-Class Honours
item.description: My name is Enoch Adeagbo. In 2021, at the age of 14, I was refused admission because I was too young. I was very sad because the reason had nothing to do with my academic ability. My parents encouraged me to apply to another university, and I eventually gained admission to Ajayi Crowther University (ACU), Oyo, at the age of 14. On Wednesday, 25 November 2026, at 19, I will graduate from ACU with First Class Honours in Civil Engineering, having earned a CGPA of 4.79 out of 5.00, as the second-best student in my department and the third-best student in the Faculty of Engineering. If I had given up and not applied to another school, I might not be here today sharing my journey. Where it all began As a child, I often accompanied my father to construction sites. I enjoyed watching structures take shape from foundation stage to completion. My interest in how buildings were designed and constructed gradually developed into a desire to become an engineer. At 14, however, I was considerably younger than most of my course mates. People frequently reminded me of my age, and I had to adjust. I learnt to focus on my studies, take part in university activities and make the most of the opportunity I had been given. In the 2022/2023 session, at 15, I received the Overall Best Student in Engineering of the Year award at the 200-level. I had not expected it, but it was also an encouraging recognition of my work, and it motivated me to stay consistent. I learnt this in the first semester of 400 level, when I got a C in Structural Analysis, a three-unit course I thought I understood. I was very sad because the reason had nothing to do with my academic ability. My parents encouraged me to apply to another university, and I eventually gained admission to Ajayi Crowther University (ACU), Oyo, at the age of 14. In the 2022/2023 session, at 15, I received the Overall Best Student in Engineering of the Year award at the 200-level. I had not expected it, but it was also an encouraging recognition of my work, and it motivated me to stay consistent. The C that taught me something But being interested in a course does not necessarily mean you’d understand it completely. I learnt this in the first semester of 400 level, when I got a C in Structural Analysis, a three-unit course I thought I understood. I was surprised because I had been confident in my knowledge of the course. That experience made me reflect on my approach to studying. I became more deliberate about understanding concepts rather than simply assuming I had mastered them. Studying with a group and teaching my coursemates also became valuable. Explaining a topic to someone else also helped me understand the course more. More than lectures Beyond the classroom, I served as the Academic Officer of the Nigerian Universities Engineering Students’ Association (NUESA), ACU Chapter, for the 2025/2026 session. I am grateful to my parents, who made sure I did not have to worry about finances while pursuing my education. Their support allowed me to concentrate on my studies and other responsibilities without the additional burden of financial concerns. Learning on real construction sites My engineering education has also involved practical experiences outside the university. In 2023, during my internship at T.E.A.M. (Nigeria) Limited, I was exposed to engineering consultancy in the construction of Obafemi Awolowo railway infrastructure in Ibadan. In 2024, I worked on drainage construction at LIDAMYT Global Contracting Services. I subsequently completed a six-month structural design internship in 2025 at Basit Opeloyeru and Associates, where I worked on structural modelling, analysis, design and detailing, alongside exposure to construction projects through site visits. Since July 2026, I have been working as an Engineering Intern at GLIC, gaining further practical experience on five-storey and seven-storey reinforced concrete buildings. My responsibilities have included supervising aspects of construction such as ribbed slab works, shear walls, staircases and roof structures. Initially, I felt inexperienced when I was given on-site supervisory responsibilities, and instructing older artisans. However, as I became more experienced with construction processes and gained practical exposure, my confidence gradually improved. The experience has helped me understand the responsibility involved in ensuring that construction activities follow engineering drawings and specifications. What comes next I hope to pursue postgraduate studies abroad through a scholarship opportunity. My ambition is to continue developing in structural engineering while also exploring research and professional opportunities in water resources engineering. I hope to build a career that combines professional practice, research and meaningful contributions to infrastructure and environmental development. I am grateful to my project supervisor, Engr. Dr A.T. Adeyokunnu, as well as the lecturers and friends who contributed to my university experience. item.title: Timothy Weah: ‘I don’t want to beg to be back in the national team’
item.description: Winger has not played for the USMNT since the World Cup and believes good club form is his route back into the squad This was the USMNT’s summer. By extension, it was also that of the 26 players selected by Mauricio Pochettino to represent the nation at a home World Cup. It didn’t live up to expectations for all of them, and certainly not for Timothy Weah. “Obviously this summer wasn’t the best for me,” he says. Weah was one of eight players in the squad to have started all four of the US’s matches in Qatar in 2022. He remained a regular heading into this tournament but would ultimately start only one game in a campaign that came to an end at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 . “In every career you have moments where you’re a bit down, and you’re a bit in your head about things. I think the World Cup was definitely that for me,” Weah says. “On a personal level, I had to take a back seat and figure out where my place was in the squad.” Continue reading...

item.title: The ten best time travel movies to buy and own on Blu-ray and 4K UHD Blu-ray this Black Friday
item.description: Love time travel movies? You're not alone and, as a sci-fi staple, cinema has no shortage of timey-wimey greats. It's Black Friday week and many of these titles are now deeply discounted. So, I picked out the ten time travel movies you need to own, from classic blockbusters like Back to the Future, through to modern gems such as Needle in a Timestack, where the only obstacle to time travel is your bank balance. We do mean own, too. All too often, we've sat down to rewatch a film to find it's vanished from our streaming service. At best, it's rematerialized on a different streaming service; at worst, it's been exterminated as some media conglomerate's tax write-off. Even 'buying' a movie, you're just getting a license that can be revoked at any time. The solution? By buying these time travel movies on Blu-ray or 4K UHD Blu-ray, they'll still be sitting on your shelf ready to watch and rewatch for years, even decades, from now. item.title: Debo Adedayo (Mr Macaroni) Joins the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts in the UK
item.description: Debo Adedayo (Mr Macaroni) joins the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts following his Master’s degree graduation in London. Photo Credit: Debo Adedayo/Instagram Have you been keeping up with Debo Adedayo lately? Because the Nigerian actor, content creator and activist—popularly known as Mr Macaroni —just added another major feather to his cap. Debo has officially joined the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts (RSA), a UK-based institution recognised globally for bringing together changemakers across the arts, social innovation and public life. Sharing the news with his followers, Debo kept his message warm and forward-looking: I am elated to join the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts. Looking forward to learning, sharing and collaborating with artists from around the world who are passionate about impacting our society for good. This recognition arrives right on the heels of a busy, rewarding season for the entertainer in London. Earlier this month, Debo graduated with a Master of Arts with Distinction in Performance (Acting) from the Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts, validated by the University of East Anglia, in the United Kingdom. During his postgraduate training at Mountview, he also made his UK stage debut in July, starring as Lord Commander Thomas Fairfax in Howard Brenton’s historical play 55 Days at The Backstage Theatre in Peckham, London. Debo Adedayo brings historical figure Lord Commander Thomas Fairfax to life in James Yeatman’s stage direction of 55 Days at Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts. Photo Credit: Debo Adedayo/Instagram Long before stepping onto the London theatre stage, Debo Adedayo (born Adebowale Babatunde Adedayo ) earned his first degree in Theatre Arts and Film Studies from Redeemer’s University in 2018. Millions first came to love him in 2019 through his satirical comedy skits—creating memorable characters like Daddy Wa and Professor Hard Life—while he has steadily built an acclaimed Nollywood film career alongside his civic advocacy in Nigeria. Debo Adedayo (Mr Macaroni) holds his Master of Arts with Distinction certificate awarded by the University of East Anglia through Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts. item.title: The Design Table 2026 by So.Me Solutions: African Fashion in the Spotlight with $7,000 in Award Support for Emerging Designers
item.description: The Design Table 2026 brought together some of the voices, ideas and creative forces shaping African fashion for an afternoon of industry exchange, recognition and conversation. The annual cultural platform, produced by So.Me Solutions, welcomed designers, fashion entrepreneurs, industry leaders, media personalities and fashion enthusiasts for its latest edition. Held at GRAS Lagos, Victoria Island, during Lagos Fashion Week, this year’s gathering explored the people, perspectives and opportunities influencing the future of African fashion. The event also marked a significant milestone for So.Me Solutions, which celebrates 10 years as a 360 communications agency. Among the guests were Folake Amber (Tiffany Amber), Bola Balogun (Glam Brand), Sharon Adeleke, Beverly Naya, Awed by Moni, Marvy Olugu (House of Marvee) and Funmi Ford , alongside other familiar faces from across fashion, entertainment and the creative scene. A Seat at the Table for the Next Generation A major highlight of this year’s edition was the Next Gen Design Impact Award, which received 101 applications from emerging designers. Following the selection process, three finalists, Sultana, Dimeji Ilori and Bjuv Woman , were shortlisted for the award. The finalists were evaluated by a five-member jury comprising Dr. Yetty Ogunnubi, Odio Mimonet, Eniafe Momodu, Ugonna-Ora Owoh and Yoanna “Pepper”, with guests also participating in the voting process. Bhuv Woman emerged as the winner, receiving the $5,000 grand prize funded by Vlisco, Patrón and Culture Lab. In addition, Odio Mimonet extended a further $2,000 in award support, bringing the total prize support associated with the award to $7,000. Beyond the financial support, the winning package includes mentorship, industry access and opportunities to further advance the designer’s work. The announcement was an emotional moment for Bhuv Woman, who was visibly moved as she received the recognition and expressed gratitude to the organisers. Through the award, The Design Table continues to create opportunities for emerging designers to gain visibility, access and recognition while connecting them with established voices and resources within the fashion industry. Who Gets to Shape the Future of African Fashion? The conversations continued with a speakers session titled “ Who Gets to Shape the Future of African Fashion?” , moderated by Yvan Otu and featured Mai Atafo , founder of ATAFO; Ezinne Chinkata , founder of Zinkata; Sacha Okoh, fashion entrepreneur and creative director of Viva; Kiki Osinbajo , founder of CIAR; and Tess Tanaka, founder of Moda54. The session explored how African fashion can move beyond being treated as a niche category and become more firmly integrated into the wider global fashion landscape. Discussions touched on what it takes for African brands to be stocked, worn and embraced as part of everyday fashion, alongside the realities of production, pricing, distribution, customer experience and access to markets. item.title: Trump, Nvidia and power: could we be nearing the end of tech’s Gilded Age?
item.description: Oligarchs believe they’re untouchable – the blue wave offers hope that the rampant corruption of the Trump era may soon be over Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive? One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after the board reinstated Jensen Huang to the CEO suite. The market gave the move a fat thumbs-up, boosting Nvidia’s share price by about a third. Shareholders, whose interests the board is meant to represent, are surely happy. But like Fifa’s controversial decision to defer the one-match suspension of US forward Folarin Balogun after receiving a red card for a foul on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tarik Muharemović during the World Cup over the summer, Huang’s absolution might backfire. item.title: Danielle Adewusi Honours Benin Kingdom Royalty in a Self-Designed National Costume at Miss Universe 2026
item.description: Danielle Adewusi displays the sweeping circular halo backpiece and floor-length beaded train of her Benin-inspired national costume. A little Benin royalty on the Miss Universe stage? Danielle Adewusi is bringing it to Puerto Rico. For the 75th edition of the competition in San Juan, Miss Universe Nigeria 2026 has arrived at the National Costume runway with Daughter of the Coral Throne, an Edo-inspired creation that brings the history of the ancient Benin Kingdom into the spotlight. And in case you missed that detail, Danielle designed the entire look herself. Now, where do we begin with this costume? The red coral beads are everywhere, from the sheer-panelled corset bodysuit and its sweetheart neckline, trimmed with gold-toned cowrie shells, to the floor-sweeping beaded overskirt and train. Look a little closer and there’s a miniature Queen Idia mask emblem at the hip. Danielle Adewusi holds her gold ceremonial staff diagonally across Daughter of the Coral Throne against a waterside garden backdrop. Then comes the fan-shaped coral bead headpiece, followed by a sweeping circular halo backpiece with cascading bead fringes. A tall gold ceremonial staff, topped with a sculpted Queen Idia mask, completes the look. Sculpted bronze-gold motifs and thousands of beads bring the whole tribute together, with each detail drawing from the artistry and royal traditions of the Benin Kingdom. Danielle Adewusi pairs warm bronzed makeup and sleek cornrows with red coral beadwork and gold cowrie detailing. Of course, Danielle isn’t leaving us to admire the costume without knowing what inspired it. She shared the story behind Daughter of the Coral Throne, explaining how she wanted to honour her Edo heritage and celebrate a kingdom whose history and identity remain, even after many of its treasures were taken: For my Miss Universe National Costume, I honour my Edo heritage and the extraordinary legacy of the ancient Kingdom of Benin, one of Africa’s greatest civilisations… Daughter of the Coral Throne reimagines the splendour of Edo royalty through contemporary African couture. Thousands of coral-inspired beads celebrate the prestige and authority of Benin royalty, while gold detailing pays tribute to the kingdom’s master craftsmen. The circular backpiece symbolises the continuity of our ancestry, radiating across generations. In my hand, a golden ceremonial staff honours the Oba of Benin, representing leadership, royal authority and an unbroken lineage. And as I follow in my mother’s footsteps, 35 years after she wore the Miss Universe Nigeria crown, I am reminded that legacy is not simply inherited. It is preserved, honoured and carried forward. item.content:encoded: Danielle Adewusi displays the sweeping circular halo backpiece and floor-length beaded train of her Benin-inspired national costume. A little Benin royalty on the Miss Universe stage? Danielle Adewusi is bringing it to Puerto Rico. For the 75th edition of the competition in San Juan, Miss Universe Nigeria 2026 has arrived at the National Costume runway with Daughter of the Coral Throne, an Edo-inspired creation that brings the history of the ancient Benin Kingdom into the spotlight. And in case you missed that detail, Danielle designed the entire look herself. Now, where do we begin with this costume? The red coral beads are everywhere, from the sheer-panelled corset bodysuit and its sweetheart neckline, trimmed with gold-toned cowrie shells, to the floor-sweeping beaded overskirt and train. Look a little closer and there’s a miniature Queen Idia mask emblem at the hip. Danielle Adewusi holds her gold ceremonial staff diagonally across Daughter of the Coral Throne against a waterside garden backdrop. Then comes the fan-shaped coral bead headpiece, followed by a sweeping circular halo backpiece with cascading bead fringes. A tall gold ceremonial staff, topped with a sculpted Queen Idia mask, completes the look. Sculpted bronze-gold motifs and thousands of beads bring the whole tribute together, with each detail drawing from the artistry and royal traditions of the Benin Kingdom. Danielle Adewusi pairs warm bronzed makeup and sleek cornrows with red coral beadwork and gold cowrie detailing. Of course, Danielle isn’t leaving us to admire the costume without knowing what inspired it. She shared the story behind Daughter of the Coral Throne, explaining how she wanted to honour her Edo heritage and celebrate a kingdom whose history and identity remain, even after many of its treasures were taken: For my Miss Universe National Costume, I honour my Edo heritage and the extraordinary legacy of the ancient Kingdom of Benin, one of Africa’s greatest civilisations… Daughter of the Coral Throne reimagines the splendour of Edo royalty through contemporary African couture. Thousands of coral-inspired beads celebrate the prestige and authority of Benin royalty, while gold detailing pays tribute to the kingdom’s master craftsmen. The circular backpiece symbolises the continuity of our ancestry, radiating across generations. In my hand, a golden ceremonial staff honours the Oba of Benin, representing leadership, royal authority and an unbroken lineage. And as I follow in my mother’s footsteps, 35 years after she wore the Miss Universe Nigeria crown, I am reminded that legacy is not simply inherited. It is preserved, honoured and carried forward. Danielle Adewusi honours her Edo heritage in Daughter of the Coral Throne ahead of the Miss Universe 2026 finale There’s a personal connection to this Miss Universe journey, too. Danielle, a 29-year-old Lagos-born medical doctor and King’s College London graduate, won Miss Universe Nigeria 2026 in September, following in the footsteps of her mother, Tonia Okogbenin , who represented Nigeria at the competition in 1991. She’s also pursuing her medical career and her women’s health initiative, Scrub the Stigma. Now, she’s carrying that family history with her as she joins 116 contestants from around the world, including 17 African queens , ahead of the grand finale, tomorrow, 24 November, in Puerto Rico. Danielle Adewusi showcases the red coral beadwork, gold cowrie shells, and sculpted Queen Idia motif of her Miss Universe National Costume. Miss Universe Nigeria 2026 Danielle Adewusi presents her self-designed Benin Kingdom national costume, Daughter of the Coral Throne. *** Photo Credit: Danielle Adewusi/Instagram The post Danielle Adewusi Honours Benin Kingdom Royalty in a Self-Designed National Costume at Miss Universe 2026 appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: Will astronauts farm on the moon? Scientists successfully grow potatoes in simulated lunar dust
item.description:
Julian Dossett is a freelance writer living in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He primarily covers the rocket industry and space exploration and, in addition to science writing, contributes travel stories to New Mexico Magazine. In 2022 and 2024, his travel writing earned IRMA Awards. Previously, he worked as a staff writer at CNET. He graduated from Texas State University in San Marcos in 2011 with a B.A. in philosophy. He owns a large collection of sci-fi pulp magazines from the 1960s.

It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon. To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal. "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement . "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon." To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith , the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. The moon contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions. The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil. Oregon State University researchers David Handy and Aymeric Goyer studying potatoes grown in lunar regolith. (Image credit: Aymeric Goyer/David Handy/OSU) "We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, said in the same statement. The idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth. NASA funding supported this research.

item.title: Join our free Space.com membership giveaway for a chance to win this Dwarflab mini smart telescope worth $419!
item.description:
Tariq is the Editor-in-Chief of Space.com based out of our New York City office and joined the team in 2001, first as an intern and staff writer, and later as an editor. He covers human spaceflight, exploration and space science, as well as skywatching and entertainment. He became Space.com's Managing Editor in 2009 and Editor-in-Chief in 2019. In October 2022, Tariq received the Harry Kolcum Award for excellence in space reporting from the National Space Club Florida Committee. In June 2025, the National Space Society awarded him the Space Pioneer Award for Excellence in Mass Media at the International Space Development Conference in Orlando, Florida.

Hailing from Stockton, California (where he attended the same high school as NASA astronaut Jose Hernandez), Tariq studied print journalism and astronomy at the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, earning a bachelor's degree in journalism in 1999 along with a minor in astronomy. He then served as a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering education and city beats in La Habra and Fullerton in Orange County for the Our Times sections.

In 2000, Tariq became the city reporter for the Huntington Beach Independent, a weekly publication of the Los Angeles Times, covering local politics and events, crime, business and environmental issues. He left the Los Angeles Times in 2001 to study science journalism at New York University, where he earned a master's degree in 2002 from NYU's Science and Environmental Reporting Program (now the Science, Health and Environmental Reporting Program) under the direction of space reporter William Burrows.

Tariq first joined Space.com as an intern in September 2001 while also serving as a research assistant for nutrition writer Gary Taubes and writing freelance projects, where his work appeared in The Scientist and Laboratory Equipment Magazine. He became a full-time reporter covering spaceflight in 2004, with this first launch being NASA's STS-114 Return to Flight mission in July 2005.

Tariq is also an Eagle Scout (yes, he has the Space Exploration merit badge) and went to Space Camp four times as a kid and a fifth time as an adult. When not writing about space, you can find Tariq watching the latest Star Trek TV series, sci-fi movies and reading about hippos, his favorite animal. You can find Tariq at Space.com and as the co-host to the This Week In Space podcast with space historian Rod Pyle on the TWiT network. To see his latest project, you can follow Tariq on Twitter @tariqjmalik.

Our Space.com Community team has launched a new giveaway exclusively for our Space+ members, and you can join for free now for a chance to win one of two Dwarflab mini smart telescopes, each worth $419. The Dwarflab giveaway is open to U.S. residents only and runs though Jan. 4, 2027. To enter, you only need to sign up for a Space.com Plus (Space+) club membership, which is free, by entering your email on our contest entry page here . (The rules and eligibility requirements are listed there). Already a Space+ member (hey, thanks!), you can still enter by entering the email associated with your membership on the entry page. If you're unfamiliar with Space+, it's a free membership program where space fans like yourself can unlock badges for reading Space.com articles, play space-themed games and test your space smarts with our cosmic quizzes. You can also sign up for one (or all) of our Space.com newsletters through Space+ to make sure you're up to date on the latest space news and discoveries, must-see skywatching events and more. While this Dwarflab smart telescope giveaway is our first contest, it won't be the last. Keep in mind, your entry is for a chance to win one of the two telescopes and there will be two U.S. winners in all. Jamie Carter Jamie Carter Jamie Carter If you're curious about why we picked Dwarflab's portable telescopes as a prize, check out our Dwarflab Mini smart telescope review to learn more. We found the ultra-compact 30-mm refractor telescope to be one of the most portable smart telescopes around, and an affordable entry-level option for stargazers hoping to break into smart telescope astrophotography on a budget. So if you're new to our Space+ crew, welcome aboard, and if you're a returning member entering the Dwarflab drawing, good luck! We'll announce the winners in January 2027 via our contest page.

item.title: The 2035 Women’s World Cup has huge potential for women and girls in UK
item.description: Maximising the societal impact of the tournament, especially combating misogyny, should be a top priority The announcement that the 2035 Women’s World Cup will be hosted in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland has finally come and, if we aim high enough, it could have a massive societal impact. Confirmation was a foregone conclusion – the UK was the only bidder – but that did not mean the submission was complacent or lacked ambition. Continue reading...

item.title: Baby News and Beautiful Blue! Mitchel Ukachukwu Is Expecting Her First Child
item.description: Mitchel Ukachukwu celebrates her pregnancy announcement in a strapless pleated royal blue gown and neck scarf. Baby news and a beautiful maternity reveal? Congratulations are certainly in order for Mitchel Ukachukwu (née Ihezue )! The former Most Beautiful Girl in Nigeria (MBGN) and Miss Universe Nigeria titleholder is expecting her first child, and she’s sharing the lovely news with photographs that have us smiling and admiring her royal blue maternity look. If this is how Mitchel is introducing us to her maternity style, we’re already looking forward to more. For her pregnancy announcement, Mitchel slipped into a strapless, floor-length royal blue gown crafted from finely pleated, semi-sheer organza. The sweetheart neckline is gathered into a knot just above her baby bump, while the skirt falls into soft pleats, opening into a high front slit. She added a matching pleated neck scarf that flows into a long cape, with sweeping lengths of royal blue fabric suspended around her to complete the setting. Mitchel Ukachukwu marks her pregnancy reveal in a pleated royal blue gown with sweeping fabric waves. We also love how the beauty details bring everything together: chestnut-brown hair in glossy, side-parted Hollywood waves, soft bronzed makeup and understated gold jewellery. And, of course, those sweet photographs of her cradling her bump make the announcement all the more lovely. Many of us first got to know Mitchel as Mitchel Ihezue when she won the Most Beautiful Girl in Nigeria crown in 2017, before going on to claim the Miss Universe Nigeria title in 2023. Her pregnancy announcement comes nearly three years after she married Nigerian billionaire businessman and Prince Nicholas Ukachukwu , popularly known as Ikukuoma. The couple celebrated their union in December 2023 with traditional and white wedding ceremonies in Anambra State and are now preparing to welcome their first child. Mitchel Ukachukwu cradles her baby bump while wearing a knotted sweetheart royal blue gown and gold accessories. Sharing the news, Mitchel wrote, “Soooo….we cooked! The bestowment of God’s goodness. God is Faithful.” And they really did cook! With their first child on the way, Mitchel and Nicholas are getting ready for a new chapter together. We can’t be the only ones already looking forward to seeing how Mitchel styles her baby bump, can we? Mitchel Ukachukwu showcases the sheer pleated skirt and flowing cape of her royal blue maternity outfit. *** Photo Credit: Mitchel Ukachukwu/Instagram The post Baby News and Beautiful Blue! Mitchel Ukachukwu Is Expecting Her First Child appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .
